News.title: Man found dead inside burning car in Portadown as police seal off scene
News.content:
Man found dead inside burning car in Portadown as police seal off scene

Police are still investigating what happened to the car for it to be set alight

View Image The body of a man was found inside a burning car in Portadown on Saturday night. (Image: NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Police are investigating after the body of a man was discovered inside a burning car in Northern Ireland.

‌



Local police in Portadown, Co Armagh, said the victim was found inside a car on fire in the Harford Street area of the town on Saturday night. He was pronounced dead at the scene.

‌



Firefighters swarmed the scene at around 10pm where crews managed to extinguish the blaze, reports Belfast Live.

‌



“Ammunition technical officers were also tasked to the scene to conduct relevant inquiries – we can confirm there is no risk to the public,” they said.

“Significant damage was caused to the car, as well as a number of windows smashed and scorch damage observed to a neighbouring property in the area.”

Police added: “Sadly, we can confirm the body of a man who was located inside the vehicle.

‌



“He was pronounced deceased at the scene and a post-mortem examination will be carried out in due course to determine the cause of death.

“The circumstances surrounding what happened are still under investigation and inquiries are ongoing to determine the cause of the fire.

“We would appeal to anyone who was in the area and witnessed what happened to make contact with us on 101.”

‌



DUP Upper Bann MP Carla Lockhart added it was a very sad morning in Portadown.

“First and foremost, my thoughts and prayers are with the family and loved ones of the deceased. Behind this news is a family facing the most devastating circumstances, and they should be very much in our thoughts this morning,” she said.

“A police cordon remains in place and the circumstances surrounding the man’s death are not yet known. It is extremely important that the PSNI are given the time and space necessary to carry out a full and thorough investigation.

Article continues below

“I would appeal to everyone to please avoid speculation on social media, particularly around the identity of the deceased or the circumstances surrounding what has happened.

“Speculation helps no one and can cause enormous additional distress to a family at an already incredibly difficult time.

“Anyone who witnessed anything or has information which may assist the investigation should please come forward to the PSNI.”

News.title: 'I'm a vet and these dog breeds hate loud owners'
News.content:
'I'm a vet and these dog breeds hate loud owners'

Not every dog loves big energy - some prefer gentle sounds

View 6 Images Some dogs prefer a calm environment (Image: Getty)

A vet has revealed the dog breeds that hate loud, over-the-top owners. While some dogs love big energy, squealing greetings and dramatic “who's a good boy?!” praise, others absolutely can’t stand it.

‌



According to health pet brand Pooch & Mutt, certain breeds are naturally sensitive, noise‑averse or easily overwhelmed. This means that instead of leaning in, they’re more likely to retreat when people get louder.

‌



Pooch & Mutts resident vet, Dr Linda Simons says: "People assume all dogs love loud praise and over‑the‑top affection. But some breeds prefer calm voices, gentle affection and predictable energy.

‌



"When owners get loud or overly enthusiastic, these dogs can become stressed, confused or even a little embarrassed." But what breeds are most likely to hate loud, chaotic people - and why?

Greyhounds

View 6 Images Fast on the track but chill at home (Image: Getty)

Greyhounds are famously gentle, sensitive dogs that tend to thrive in calm homes. They usually respond best to soft voices, slow movements and a peaceful routine rather than big, noisy greetings.

‌



Loud noise can be a problem as many greyhounds are easily overstimulated. Their sensitive temperament means sudden shouting, squealing or chaotic environments can make them anxious or keen to move away.

Whippets

View 6 Images Pooch and Mutt's resident vet, Doctor Linda Simon (Image: Pooch and Mutt)

Whippets love affection - but not chaos. They’re typically gentle, easily startled dogs that do best with calm, cosy energy and low-key routines rather than loud, hyped-up greetings.

‌



Loud noise can be a problem because this breed can be noise-sensitive, and their soft, sensitive nature means sudden shouting or squealing can overwhelm them, making them flinch, freeze, or retreat to a quieter spot.

Basset Hounds

View 6 Images Slow, steady and unbothered - the laid-back patient vets love (Image: Getty)

Bassets don’t hate loud humans, they just don’t see the point. They prefer quiet reassurance over dramatic praise. They hate loud noises because of their low‑energy temperament and dislike of overstimulation.

‌



Shih Tzus

View 6 Images Cheerful, calm and adaptable - a little dog who handles it all (Image: Getty)

Shih Tzus love affection, but not chaos. They’re happiest when life feels like a gentle pamper session and therefore hate sudden noise, and prefer calm handling.

Newfoundlands

View 6 Images These dogs are known for their calm nature (Image: Getty)

‌



Newfoundlands are famously calm, steady dogs that tend to prefer slow, soothing affection over high-pitched excitement and frantic greetings. Louid noises can be an issue as, despite their size, some Newfoundlands can be noise-sensitive.

This means their laid-back temperament can make sudden shouting or squealing feel jarring. Because of this, they may turn away, step back, or seek a quieter corner.

Three common traits

Dr Linda says these dogs often share three traits that make them more likely to recoil from loud, over-the-top humans:

Article continues below

Noise sensitivity: loud voices can feel overwhelming or stressful.

loud voices can feel overwhelming or stressful. Low reactivity: they prefer calm environments and predictable energy.

they prefer calm environments and predictable energy. Gentle temperament: big enthusiasm can feel like too much.

"These dogs aren’t being rude or aloof", Linda explains, adding: “They’re simply wired to prefer calm, quiet interactions. Loud praise or chaotic affection can make them feel overwhelmed rather than loved.

"Dogs who favour gentle energy tend to enjoy slow, steady strokes, soft voices and predictable movements. It helps them feel safe, relaxed and understood."

News.title: F1 Academy star, 16, reaches 155mph on racetracks - but hasn't passed driving test yet
News.content:
F1 Academy star, 16, reaches 155mph on racetracks - but hasn't passed driving test yet

Lisa Billard, 16, is taking part in F1 Academy, a female-only racing championship, and hopes to qualify for Formula 1 in the future

View 5 Images The young driver still doesn't hold a valid driving licence for roads but can drive a racecar

Speeding around racetracks at over 150mph, it's hard to believe that teenage motorsport prodigy Lisa Billard doesn't even have a valid driving licence yet. At just 16-years-old, the French driver is currently in the middle of high-pressure race season, while simultaneously trying to learn how to drive a normal car.

‌



"I've done my first lesson driving on the road and it was really strange as you have to drive at 30mph," Lisa laughed. "My driving instructor knows I am a racing driver, so he is very strict with me when it comes to the speed."

‌



Lisa currently drives in Formula 4, where her car reaches top speeds of 155mph - in stark contrast to the small Renault Clio she's learning in for her test. She said: "I am learning new things because it's a manual so it's different to Formula 4 and all the rules are different. There is no flag and you have to stop at the traffic lights."

‌



Max Verstappen told blunt truth about his F1 career as Red Bull quit decision looms READ MORE :

View 5 Images The 16-year-old is currently learning how to drive on the roads

Originally from Normandy, France, Lisa's passion for motorsports began at seven when she started go-karting alongside her dad.

Standing out as a young girl in a heavily male-dominated sport presented early hurdles. "I've always loved speed and adrenaline. Starting at seven years old as the only girl was difficult," Lisa told Daily Mirror. "The boys were a lot more aggressive with me on the track because they didn't want to have a girl in front of them."

‌



Undeterred, Lisa carried on, and last year, she stepped onto the global stage as the youngest-ever Wild Card driver for Round 6 of the F1 Academy season in Singapore.

The F1 Academy is an all-women driving school designed to develop young drivers aged 16 to 25, offering crucial support for rising talent.

"It's really good [in the academy] to have other girls who are doing the same thing as me," Lisa said.

‌



View 5 Images The young female driver is currently racing as part of the Formula One Academy

"We are all chasing the same role and it feels like a family. We understand each other and [know how]difficult [the] path [can be] for a girl." Her goal is to break into Formula 1 - a sport that currently has no female drivers on the starting grid - and compete at the highest level. "My goal is one day to become a Formula One driver, and not only to just do it as a girl, but to be one of the best drivers in the world," Lisa said.

"People assume we just want to go fast, but the goal is to be the best on the track." Reaching that level requires an immense level of preparation, that goes beyond spending hours behind the wheel.

‌



When she isn't driving on the track or training in a simulator, Lisa stays fit through rock climbing. During a race weekend, temperatures inside a cockpit can peak between 50°C and 60°C due to engine heat, hot asphalt, and the thick fireproof suits drivers wear.

5 View 5 Images Lisa's passion for racing started at a young age thanks to her dad 5 View 5 Images With no current female drivers in the competition, Lisa hopes one day she can join the men in the race

Article continues below

The extreme conditions cause drivers to lose up to four litres of fluid over a single race weekend.

"Losing that much water means I am quite sweaty after a race," Lisa said. "You need to make sure you are very hydrated before to make sure you have enough endurance. Being sponsored by Gatorade works well for this as they always help me keep well-hydrated and I have a specialist tracking everything."

Oozing coolness as she zips across the tarmac, Lisa's passion for racing slows no signs of cooling down - and she is just getting started.

News.title: Fifty years ago she went on holiday - and was never seen again
News.content:
Fifty years ago she went on holiday - and was never seen again

Police have issued a fresh appeal for any information on a British woman who vanished while on a holiday in France five decades ago

View 2 Images Sarjit Kaur Mann was 20 when she vanished 50 years ago (Image: Family Handout/PA Wire)

Police have issued a fresh appeal for information to help solve the mystery disappearance of a 20-year-old British woman who vanished abroad 50 years ago.

‌



Sarjit Kaur Mann, from Birmingham, was last seen in September 1976, after she went on holiday with her family to the south of France. The 20-year-old had been a student at the University of Birmingham and was with her family in Antibes when she asked to stay behind when they were heading home. The student told her family that she wanted to spend time with people she had met and visit some of the local museums.

‌



Sarjit's family arrived back in the UK but the young woman was never seen again.

‌



View 2 Images The young woman had been on holiday in Antibes, France, when she disappeared (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

West Midlands Police issued a renewed appeal on Saturday, which would be Sarjit's 70th birthday, making a plea for any information which might help shed light on her disappearance.

Cops said a woman Sarjit met called Jane is said to have phoned the family a few days after they returned home saying Sarjit had drowned, before hanging up.

‌



Pc Shaun Reeve, from the West Midlands Police missing person investigation unit, said: "What happened to Sarjit in France remains a mystery and we have always kept an open mind.

"At the time, Sarjit was said to have met a group of young women of a similar age, one of whom was called Jane.

"We believe Jane called Sarjit's family a few days after they returned home and told them their daughter had drowned before hanging up.

‌



"Whether this caller was Jane or not, we do not know. The caller was never identified and Sarjit has never been found.

"What we are hoping for is that someone who knew Sarjit and her family at the time might be able to help us piece together more about her life around the time she went missing.

"Even though this was a long time ago, we will never stop investigating any new information we receive as we try to bring some answers, or closure, to Sarjit’s family after nearly 50 years."

Article continues below

West Midlands Police have asked anybody who thinks they can help in this probe to call the team directly on 0121 626 7003.

News.title: Four groups getting hundreds less from benefit this summer
News.content:
Four groups getting hundreds less from benefit this summer

Some of the rules for Universal Credit changed in April, affecting everyone applying for the benefit now

View 3 Images The April rule change is affecting everyone applying for Universal Credit's health element now (Image: GETTY)

Universal Credit’s health element underwent a major revamp in April, affecting who qualifies and how much they will receive. As a result, certain groups of people applying for the benefit now will be getting around half as much from the health element as others.

‌



Universal Credit’s health element, also known as Limited Capability for Work and Work-related Activity (LWCRA), is a vital support for over two million claimants. It adds an extra amount onto the monthly payments for people with health conditions and disabilities if it interferes with their ability to work.

‌



The extra payment used to be paid at a flat rate of £423.27 per month for everyone that qualified. One of the first changes implemented in April was the introduction of a lower rate worth only £217.26, roughly half of what the payment used to be.

‌



There are four specific groups of people that will get the new lower rate and receive £206 less each month than their peers who qualified before the rule change.

View 3 Images Qualifying for the health element can also change your Claimant Agreement (Image: GETTY)

You will get the lower amount of LCWRA if all the following apply:

‌



you declare a health condition or disability on or after 6 April 2026

you do not have a severe, lifelong health condition

you are not nearing the end of your life

your partner, if you have one, is not entitled to the higher LCWRA amount

In order to get the higher rate, equivalent to the rate that every eligible claimant received before the rule change, you must done at least one of the following before April 6, 2026:

Told the DWP about your condition

Already getting LCWRA

Had the ‘support group’ component of income-related Employment and Support Allowance and continue to get it until you claim Universal Credit

‌



Additionally, people who have a severe health condition or disability that’s unlikely to change or are nearing the end of their life can qualify for the higher rates regardless of when they informed the DWP or applied for benefits.

Anyone that receives the extra payment must also keep the DWP updated if their health condition changes. This can include if it gets better, worse or if you’re diagnosed with something new.

View 3 Images Only certain people can now qualify for the health element (Image: GETTY)

Article continues below

The new health element criteria does not affect a person’s eligibility for other elements of Universal Credit. The benefit provides a standard rate to all successful claimants as well as other add-ons depending on their circumstances.

News.title: Woman finds giant wasp nest after going on holiday - 'there are thousands'
News.content:
Woman finds giant wasp nest after going on holiday - 'there are thousands'

Eilish returned from holiday to discover thousands of wasps had made themselves at home

View 3 Images The giant wasp nest (Image: Jam Press/Eilish Rothney)

A woman returned from holiday to find thousands of wasps had moved in and constructed an enormous nest. Eilish Rothney said the creatures had sneaked in through a hole in the door frame.

‌



The reserve warden with Norfolk Wildlife Trust, returned from her holidays to find the insects had completely taken over her office at Trinity Broads. By the time she arrived back, the nest was fully formed – and the unwelcome lodgers show no signs of leaving.

‌



"The nest is in my office. They collected scraping from wood outside and meticulously built the nest and are still doing so," Eilish said.

‌



"They get in through a hole in the door frame and tolerate me opening the door, going inside and doing some work. I try not to disturb them. They do a good job controlling leaf-eating insects otherwise our trees could be bare!"

View 3 Images The wasp nest has made a right old mess

She joked: "Usually being a wildlife charity means protecting wildlife - this week it meant negotiating office space with it. Thousands of new colleagues moved in without permission, skipped recruitment entirely and ignored the office hot-desking policy.

‌



"Can't fault them on attendance, though." As Eilish spends the majority of the summer carrying out conservation work and wildlife surveys, the wasps were able to settle in and make themselves at home while she was away.

Eilish added: "In the summer I am out most of the time doing conservation work or surveys. I am the only member of staff on the reserve so it's only cleaned when I clean it.

"They started building when I was away on leave. They have been in residence for at least a month." Despite their fearsome reputation, Norfolk Wildlife Trust believes wasps deserve far greater recognition than they typically receive.

Article continues below

View 3 Images Eilish Rothney

Reserves officer Robert Morgan said that despite numerous encounters with wasps, he has a great admiration for their no-nonsense attitude. He said: "Wasp stings are an occupational hazard in wildlife conservation work.

"It's resulted in 22 stings painfully scribbled in the accident book." Norfolk Wildlife Trust stressed that wasps are vital to healthy ecosystems and urged anyone worried about a nest to seek professional guidance, as some species are harmless or rare and disturbing nests can prove dangerous.

News.title: Huge search at Weymouth beach for missing woman who 'entered sea' and 'failed to return'
News.content:
Huge search at Weymouth beach for missing woman who 'entered sea' and 'failed to return'

Police, the Coastguard, RNLI and a police helicopter are involved in a major search for a woman feared missing after entering the sea in Weymouth.

View Image A huge search has been launched for a missing woman (Image: Getty Images)

A huge search has been launched for a missing woman who was seen entering the sea at Weymouth beach and is not believed to have returned.

‌



Police, the Coastguard, RNLI and a police helicopter are involved in the search after the woman entered the water at around 11.05pm on Saturday.

‌



A member of the public raised the alarm after reportedly seeing her enter the water for Weymouth Esplanade but did not re-appear.

‌



The missing woman is described as being of average build with long hair and was seen getting into the water with a long, flowing dress which is a lighter colour at the top.

She is believed to have been on her own at the time, but none of her belongings have been found on the beach.

‌



Dorset Police said officers have been carrying out searches while growing "increasingly concerned" for the woman's welfare.

Inspector Mark Latter, of Dorset Police, said: “We are growing increasingly concerned for the woman’s welfare and are carrying out enquiries to locate her.

“The woman was on her own at the time of the incident and no belongings have been found following a search of the beach area."

Article continues below

He continued: "I am appealing to anyone who may have witnessed a woman matching the description in the Weymouth Esplanade area at the time of the incident to contact us.

“I am also directly appealing to the woman to get in touch with us if she has left the water and is safe and well.”

Anyone with information is asked to contact Dorset Police by calling 999, quoting incident number 8-598.

News.title: Warning to anyone with more than one pension pot and the checks you need to make
News.content:
Warning to anyone with more than one pension pot and the checks you need to make

Pension consolidation can make your retirement savings easier to manage - but not every pension should be transferred, as you could lose benefits

View Image Pension consolidation takes careful consideration (Image: Milan_Jovic via Getty Images)

If you've changed jobs a few times over the years, there's a good chance you've built up more than one pension pot without even realising it.

‌



One from your first job. Another from an employer you stayed with for a few years. Perhaps another from a company you barely remember working for. Before long, your retirement savings are spread across several providers, all with different charges, investments and paperwork.

‌



Bringing those pensions together, known as pension consolidation, can make your retirement savings much easier to manage and, in some cases, could even leave you better off by reducing the fees you pay.

‌



However, experts warn there's one important catch: not every pension should be transferred. Some older pensions contain valuable guarantees or benefits that could be reduced or lost if you move them.

Please note: This article is intended as general information and not personal financial advice. Whether consolidating your pensions is right for you depends on your individual circumstances. Always check what benefits you could lose before transferring any pension.

Why many people have several pension pots

Automatic enrolment means most employees are now paying into a workplace pension, which is good news for retirement savings. But every time you change jobs, you will usually leave one pension behind and start another.

‌



Over a working lifetime, it's easy to build up several pension pots and lose track of where they all are.

If you're unsure where your old pensions are, start by using the Government's free Pension Tracing Service before considering whether to consolidate them.

Could combining your pensions save you money?

Combining pensions doesn't increase the amount you've saved. If you have four pension pots worth £25,000 each, you'll still have £100,000 after transferring them into one place.

‌



Where consolidation can make a difference is through charges. If your new pension has lower annual fees than your old schemes, more of your investment returns stay invested instead of being eaten away by charges year after year.

Over 20 or 30 years, that difference can become significant. Illustrative calculations suggest that someone aged 40 with £150,000 spread across several defined contribution pensions who reduced annual charges from 1% to 0.5% and remained invested until age 65 could retire with tens of thousands of pounds more , depending on investment performance and other factors.

Consolidation can also make retirement planning easier because you'll have fewer accounts to monitor and less paperwork to keep track of.

‌



Illustrative example only: The figures above are based on hypothetical assumptions about pension charges, investment growth and the length of time the money remains invested. They are not a guarantee of future returns, and your outcome could be higher or lower.

Jasmine Birtles: 'Don't assume every pension is the same'

Jasmine Birtles, founder of MoneyMagpie, said: "The mistake isn't having several pensions. The mistake is assuming they're all the same. One old pension could be quietly charging more than it should, while another could contain guarantees that would be incredibly expensive to replace."

"Consolidating your pensions can make excellent financial sense if it reduces charges and makes your retirement savings easier to manage. But every pension deserves its own health check before you move a penny."

‌



She adds: " Your pension is one of the biggest financial assets you'll ever own. Spending a little time understanding what you've got before making any decisions could be one of the most valuable financial jobs you ever do."

Which pensions are often suitable for consolidation?

Many people choose to consolidate:

Old workplace defined contribution pensions.

pensions. Personal pensions.

Stakeholder pensions.

Auto-enrolment pensions from previous employers.

Some self-invested personal pensions (SIPPs), depending on charges and investment options.

‌



These pensions are based on the amount contributed and how investments perform. If a newer pension offers lower charges or better value, transferring may be worth considering.

Which pensions should you check very carefully?

Some pensions include valuable benefits that could be lost if they're transferred.

Final salary (defined benefit) pensions

‌



These provide a guaranteed retirement income based on your salary and years of service. They are often among the most valuable pensions available, and most people are likely to be better off keeping them unless specialist advice suggests otherwise.

Pensions with guaranteed annuity rates

Some older pensions promise a higher level of retirement income than can be bought today. Those guarantees may disappear if you transfer.

‌



With-profits pensions

Older with-profits pensions can include valuable terminal bonuses that may be reduced or lost if you move the money elsewhere.

Protected pension age

‌



Some older schemes allow you to take your pension earlier than current rules normally allow. A transfer could mean losing that protection.

Enhanced tax-free cash

Certain historic pensions allow more than the standard 25% tax-free lump sum. Moving the pension could remove this entitlement.

‌



Workplace pensions with added benefits

Some employer schemes include life insurance or ill-health benefits that don't automatically transfer with the pension.

One group should be especially careful

If you have a pension worth less than £10,000 , don't automatically assume you should combine it with your other pensions.

‌



Depending on how you plan to access your retirement savings, keeping a small pension separate can sometimes be more tax efficient under the pension "small pots" rules.

Five checks before transferring any pension

Before moving any pension, make sure you know:

What annual charges you're paying.

Whether there are exit fees.

If you'll lose guarantees or protected benefits.

Whether the new pension offers better value.

How the transfer fits into your long-term retirement plans.

‌



Before you make any decision

Take time to understand exactly what each pension offers before transferring it.

If you're unsure, consider using the free guidance available from MoneyHelper or speak to a regulated financial adviser. This is particularly important if you have a final salary pension or another scheme with valuable guarantees.

Having several pension pots isn't a problem in itself. The real issue is not knowing what you've got. For many people, consolidating straightforward defined contribution pensions can make retirement planning much simpler and may even reduce the amount paid in charges over the years.

Article continues below

But don't assume every pension belongs in the same place. Some older schemes are valuable because of the guarantees hidden inside them, not simply the amount of money they contain.

A couple of hours spent reviewing your pensions today could make your retirement easier to manage and help you avoid an expensive mistake tomorrow.

News.title: Andy Burnham to embark on cost of living tour through the UK
News.content:
The prime minister is set to announce "a series of measures to make life easier" for those struggling with the cost of living in the coming days, Downing Street says.

No 10 says Andy Burnham's plans are to "give people some room to breathe". He will also focus on ways of "improving high streets" as he embarks on a tour of the UK.

But the government is facing continued pressure over its early release scheme for prisoners in England and Wales â with criticism of the fact that two of PC Andrew Harper's killers will be eligible from next year.

Burnham is also likely to face pressure for more action on the cost of living â although significant interventions are unlikely before October's Budget.

Even then, Chancellor John Healey has made it clear he will oversee "strong fiscal discipline" â which will limit how much the government has to spend.

The prime minister has been on holiday this week, but Downing Street said he would be in "listening mode" in the coming days as he tours the UK's nations and regions and works on a "10-year plan to bring back hope".

A spokesman for the prime minister said: "He thinks Westminster has got used to telling people that everyday hassles â like hidden pricing and consumers being ripped off â must be accepted as part of life.

"He doesn't think that's right. That's why he's going to start rolling out a series of pro-consumer cost of living measures to give people some room to breathe."

The spokesman added: "He's also going to be kicking off his summer tour around the country, getting out of Westminster and meeting people where they are.

"The prime minister is going to be in listening mode to help inform his 10-year plan to bring back hope and make Britain better off."

There are, though, likely to be continued questions about the forthcoming early release scheme, due to start in October.

One of Burnham's first acts in Downing Street was to order a review which limited the range of people who would be eligible.

But those convicted of manslaughter will still qualify for the scheme â including two of the killers of PC Andrew Harper.

The prime minister has faced calls from PC Harper's family, former senior police officers and opposition politicians for them to be denied early release.

But he has said he cannot go any further without risking prison capacity. Downing Street said on Saturday night that position remained unchanged, despite reports the prime minister could revisit the case.

Despite early release schemes having been in place for England and Wales since late 2023 under the previous Conservative government, the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) has warned the prison population could overtake capacity as soon as this November.

The latest figures for England and Wales, recorded on 23 August, showed the prison population was at 86,495 - more than 97% of useable capacity.

On the cost of living plans, the Conservatives said the government's "tax hikes and red tape are hammering our high streets".

Shadow chancellor Mel Stride said: "This is breathtaking hypocrisy from Burnhamâ¦ they are forcing businesses to close, destroying jobs and driving up prices for the public.

"Meanwhile, Labour are plotting to release dangerous criminals onto our streets, leaving people feeling unsafe in their communities."

Liberal Democrat Treasury spokeswoman Daisy Cooper said struggling high street businesses "need more than a new PM embarking on a vanity tour this summer".

She said the PM should adopt the Lib Dem plan for high streets: "That means reversing the damaging jobs tax, delivering an emergency VAT cut for hospitality, replacing broken business rates and cracking down on the ghost landlords leaving our shop fronts vacant."

Reform UK's economic spokesman Robert Jenrick said: "If Andy Burnham wants to help people with the cost of living, he should scrap the green levies and taxes on energy bills and rule out tax rises at the Budget."

News.title: Killed a month after his wedding - why PC Andrew Harper's story touched so many
News.content:
On the night of 15 August 2019, Lissie Harper got a knock at the door. She thought it was her husband Andrew coming home from work.

Instead, it was uniformed officers, there to tell her that the man she had married four weeks earlier had been killed while on police duty.

"Everything I had known in my life to be true was robbed away. Every ounce of beautiful peace, gone," Lissie later said of the moment she was told.

They had met as teenagers and were together for 13 years.

In her eulogy at his funeral, Lissie recalled how Andrew would pass her notes in class.

They were, she said, "true childhood sweethearts, loving one another more and more with each passing day".

They had been about to go on their honeymoon.

But, on that night nearly seven years ago, everything changed.

The case has been back in the headlines because two of PC Harper's killers â Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole â will become eligible to be released early under government plans to tackle prison overcrowding.

As the disturbing details of the case are revisited, his family, fellow officers and the public are outraged once more â at what happened, and at the perpetrators' impending release.

PC Harper's death was brutal and devastating, causing shock, anger and an outpouring of grief across the country.

Pictures of the smiling faces of his teenage killers laughing and joking as they left court only added to that anger.

PC Harper had been about to head home at the end of a long shift when he and a colleague were called to reports of a burglary.

He was "going beyond the call of duty", the prosecutor at the Old Bailey trial in 2020 said.

During the case, haunting dashcam footage from the police patrol car was played showing the moment PC Harper confronted teenagers Henry Long, Bowers and Cole down a dark country lane. He then disappeared from view.

His ankles had got caught in a strap trailing behind the car being driven by Long that had been used to tow a stolen quad bike.

PC Harper was dragged for over a mile. He died on the road. His police badge and stab vest were found scattered along the route.

The three teenagers were tried for murder. In the end, the jury convicted Bowers and Cole of manslaughter. Long had already pleaded guilty to that offence.

It meant the jury was not sure that PC Harper's killers knew they were dragging the officer behind the car.

But the Judge, Mr Justice Edis, described it as a manslaughter case which was "very close to a case of murder" in its seriousness.

News.title: Australia is the planet's extinction hotspot, but one animal offers a glimmer of hope
News.content:
"Eyes peeled," comes the order from the front passenger seat.

Obediently, we scan the ends and tops of logs, looking between low scrub and patches of vivid wildflowers for a flash of stripes or a dart of movement.

Eluding us is the numbat, a rare Australian marsupial which could be the love-child of a chipmunk and an anteater.

Numbats were once populous across the bottom half of the continent, but Dryandra Woodland â in the south-western corner of Australia â is one of the few places they remain.

As we slowly roll along bush tracks, researchers explain how this annual trip helps plot the species' survival.

Classified as endangered until this month, numbats have been bouncing back. This team's efforts have seen them scratched off the international red list of threatened species - a rare glimmer of hope in a country facing an extinction emergency.

This part of Australia is the front line of that crisis: a last stand for many species driven to the brink by feral pests, disease, urban development, habitat destruction and climate change.

Winging over our car at one point is the endangered Carnaby's cockatoo. On an island just off the coast is one of the last surviving pockets of the world's rarest marsupial, the Gilbert's potoroo. Diving in the sapphire waters around it is the increasingly scarce Australian sea lion.

News.title: Kellie Bright to leave EastEnders after 13 years
News.content:
EastEnders star Kellie Bright is to leave the soap after playing one of its key characters, Linda Carter, for 13 years.

She arrived in Albert Square with on-screen husband Mick, portrayed by Danny Dyer, when they became the new owners of the Queen Vic pub.

Carter's matriarch character has been central to major storylines including plots about murder, sexual assault and alcoholism.

Bright said she made the "tough decision" to leave more than a year ago but "happily" agreed to stay on to be part of an "exciting storyline".

The BBC has promised "unmissable drama" before her on-screen exit, which is said to be a "while away" yet.

Executive producer Ben Wadey described the actor as being "the beating heart of EastEnders" and said she had become "a classic EastEnders icon".

Viewers have seen the much-loved character at the heart of many emotional storylines including in 2014 when she was raped by her brother-in-law Dean Wicks.

More than 7m people watched the episode which prompted dozens of complaints. The sexual assualt led to long-running story arc about family conflict and trauma.

News.title: Zendaya saw me on the red carpet and her jaw dropped - I'm still in shock
News.content:
"I can't zip this! Mummm?"

This was 29-year-old Zainab Jiwa, calling out for help squeezing into a corset while filming a "get-ready-with-me" TikTok video. It's a scene many 20-somethings still living at home will relate to.

The difference is, Zainab was on her way to the recent London premiere of The Odyssey, one of the summer's biggest blockbusters.

She was invited there as a guest and says she caught the eye of Hollywood megastar Zendaya, thanks to her custom look: a striking gold gown complete with a hood.

"She just walked past, and she saw me there. Her jaw just dropped, so did mine," Zainab tells me.

"It was just a stare-off for a minute, and she was like, 'Oh my god, amazing, amazing,' and then she just walked off."

"Iâm still in shock,â she adds. âThe thought of her noticing my outfit blew my mind."

The interaction went viral, external with 19m TikTok views. Her phone blew up.

While Zendaya has been ruling the red carpets with high-fashion "method dressing" â where stars match outfits to a film's themes â Zainab is perhaps proving that independent creators like her can give Hollywood a run for its money.

Zainab, who is Muslim and wears a hijab, is also often one of the only people covering her hair at premieres, but she says finding ways to incorporate modest wear is part of the fun.

"Even though you're covered, you can still find a way to be on theme.â

News.title: How weight-loss medication is changing relationships with alcohol
News.content:
There is a growing body of research into the link between weight-loss drugs and alcohol consumption.

The drugs, with brands including Wegovy, Mounjaro and Ozempic, contain semaglutide or tirzepatide, which mimic a natural hormone called GLP-1. This suppresses appetite and keeps people feeling fuller for longer, helping them to lose weight.

Early research suggests that because these drugs affect the reward response in the brain, they can reduce cravings for substances including alcohol and nicotine, says Dr Christian Hendershot of the University of South Carolina.

He published a small-scale study, external in 2025 in which participants with alcohol use disorder craved alcohol less while taking Ozempic. Alcohol use disorder, sometimes referred to as alcoholism, is described by the NHS as drinking in a way that is harmful.

A study, external from the University of Colorado Anschutz published last week also suggested that GLP-1 medications in pill form led to fewer days of heavy drinking in people with mild to moderate alcohol use disorder.

People taking the drugs told BBC News that alcohol had affected them in different ways: some said their cravings for it had gone, drinking had made them feel nauseous or uncomfortably full, or they had got drunk more quickly. Others said they had not noticed any effect on their relationship with alcohol.

Before she started taking Wegovy, Lisa says she drank between six and eight bottles of wine a week with friends. But she had sometimes worried about whether this was too much and whether it could damage her health.

NHS guidance, external is that people should not drink more than 14 units a week on a regular basis, which is about six medium glasses of wine or six pints. Drinking too much in the long term can lead to liver damage, high blood pressure and increased risk of cancer.

Lisa says that since starting on the medication she has more than halved her consumption. At a recent day festival, she drank three glasses of wine over the course of nine hours. Previously, she would have had two bottles plus a couple of vodka mixers, she says.

Alcohol has always been a big part of her social life and when she stopped drinking for a few weeks in the late 2010s, she realised friends had stopped inviting her to social events. It led her to start drinking again.

This time round, Lisa says that she still looks forward to drinking wine, but after having a couple of glasses she simply cannot stomach any more.

"I still feel involved in things because I'm still drinking but drinking a lot less," Lisa says.

For years, Warren Thomas, 45, from Colchester, had enjoyed an occasional beer with his family after work, as well as one or two heavy drinking sessions with his friends each month.

But when he spoke to his friends on weight-loss medication about his plans to start taking Mounjaro, they warned him that it could affect how much he drank.

Warren says he noticed the effect within 24 hours of his first dose in mid-June. "I just don't want to drink," he says. "I've just got no appetite for it."

When he went out for his friend's birthday last month, he felt "light-headed and a little bit giddy" after two beers, he says.

"My tolerance level to drinking is now zero," he says.

There is no formal advice in the British National Formulary, a guide to dispensing medicine used by doctors and pharmacists, about whether people on weight-loss drugs should stop drinking alcohol, says Prof Russell Hearn, a GP and professor of medicine at King's College London.

But he gives careful advice to his patients. "Alcohol has a lot of calories in it and if your goal is to lose weight, drinking less will definitely help you with that alongside changing your diet while you're on a GLP-1," he says.

For people like Lisa and Warren, drinking less alcohol has been a happy bonus. But recent graduate Faye Goodwin, 20, feels that it has hampered her social life.

When Faye drinks she says she gets nauseous very quickly and sometimes throws up or gets bad acid reflux.

Faye, who got in touch with BBC Your Voice, has been taking Mounjaro since she was 18 and does not really know what it is like to drink alcohol without the impact of weight-loss medication. But she says she once took a month off the jabs and was able to drink without experiencing any nausea.

News.title: Why eclipse chasers are crossing continents for solar spectacle: 'It's like the World Cup'
News.content:
On Wednesday, parts of Europe will be plunged into daytime darkness as the moon passes in front of the sun, temporarily blocking its light and casting a shadow across the continent.

For many of us, it will be a once-in-a-lifetime experience. But for some, following eclipses has become something of an addiction.

Armed with two high-spec cameras, a specialist telescope and a drone, Mark Griffiths has spent two days driving from Cheshire to Galicia - one of the best places to view the eclipse - to record the event.

It's a hobby that started six years ago, when he went to Shetland to see the northern lights - though the weather was so dreary he "didn't see anything".

But it didn't put him off and he soon found he couldn't stop. He loved the thrill of witnessing and capturing the sky's most spectacular events.

News.title: Hundreds arrested over French wildfires, but who is to blame?
News.content:
After wildfires caused more damage in France this year than at any time since World War Two, many are left asking a single question: Why?

A major driver is that climate is changing as a result of the well-documented way humanity is burning fossil fuels. Temperatures are only rising.

But with records showing that nine out of 10 French wildfires are started by humans, the government in Paris is trying to attribute blame - although it is itself accused of being underprepared for the infernos that have now scorched more than 300,000 acres this summer.

The interior ministry has announced 420 arrests of people alleged to have either started the fires deliberately or by accident. Among them are 166 minors.

In one case, a 23-year-old man has been accused of deliberately starting 10 fires in the space of five days in the south-eastern Var area last month. He faces 15 years in prison and a â¬150,000 (Â£128,000) fine, if convicted.

Many others have been tried and immediately sentenced, such as a man who received a three-year jail sentence for starting three recent fires in the Raon-L'Ãtape forest in the Vosges region.

"Only a few square metres of vegetation went up in smoke," noted L'Est RÃ©publicain, the newspaper that reported the story.

Other prosecutions have been perceived as heavy-handed and unjust. A homeless man and someone with severe autism have reportedly been handed jail terms for throwing cigarette butts.

"I was amazed at the number of arrests, it feels excessive," admits Muriel Gestas, a lawyer who has represented several people accused of arson, including two firefighters. She doubts many will lead to a conviction.

The newspaper Le Monde is also unconvinced. It questions to what extent police have examined these cases, given the short time frame.

The authorities' silence on the details - the specific charges, notably whether they involve intent and how the numbers compare with past seasons - rules out any meaningful comparison with previous years, it argues.

But Bordeaux prosecutor Renaud Gaudeul told Le Monde that a tough approach was justified by current circumstances.

"The conditions for a charge of endangering lives are met for those who throw a cigarette butt or light a barbecue in wooded areas. It only takes a tiny spark for it to start," the newspaper quoted him as saying.

News.title: Family 'devastated' as hit-and-run driver who killed boy, 13, to have early prison release
News.content:
The family of a 13-year-old boy killed in a hit-and-run say they are "devastated" after being told the driver who caused his death has had his sentence reduced.

Kaylan Hippsley died three days after being struck by a car driven by Harley Whiteman on Brecon Road in Hirwaun, Rhondda Cynon Taf, on 29 February 2024.

Whiteman was originally sentenced to six years and nine months in prison and banned from driving for eight years and four months but, after Kaylan's family appealed, High Court judges increased the sentence to nine years.

Now, the family has been told Whiteman can be released under licence as early as this autumn as part of the UK government's Sentencing Act early release scheme.

News.title: Banksy works cost public almost £150,000
News.content:
Three artworks by street artist Banksy have cost taxpayers almost Â£150,000 in cleaning operations and security so far, with the bill expected to rise.

The largest single cost relates to a mural painted on the Royal Courts of Justice in September 2025, where removal efforts and security have so far cost more than Â£85,000.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) says it has spent Â£50,000 trying to remove paint from the wall of the Grade II-listed building in Carey Street. A further Â£35,300 was spent on overtime and security costs.

The spending was disclosed to the BBC through Freedom of Information requests and is likely to reignite debate over whether Banksy's work is vandalism or valuable public art.

News.title: Charity watchdog investigates aid charity over alleged Hamas links
News.content:
A UK-based aid charity is being investigated by counter-terror police and the charity watchdog over alleged links to Hamas.

The Charity Commission launched an inquiry into Muslim faith-based charity Al-Khair Foundation on Friday.

Counter Terror Policing London (CTP) also confirmed investigations into the charity, with two search warrants on addresses in Croydon, South London.

The foundation said it is "co-operating fully" with the inquiry and had filed a serious incident report with the watchdog before it was launched.

A spokesperson for the foundation said: "Everywhere we work we are firmly committed to ensuring that the funds entrusted to us by our generous donors are used for their intended purpose: meeting the humanitarian needs of poor and marginalised people in the communities we serve.

"Al-Khair Foundation is deeply committed to supporting those in need in Gaza. Our significant support over many years has included providing food parcels, hot meals, clean water, medical aid, shelter materials, winter assistance and orphan and family support."

The Al-Khair Foundation provides emergency relief and developmental support in "some of the world's most impoverished areas", according to its website.

Hamas is designated as a terrorist organisation by the UK and US governments.

It comes after last week Mohammad Yousef Hasna, 45, from Istanbul, Turkey, was arrested in the UK over US accusations of conspiring to funnel money and supplies to Hamas through a "sham charity".

The US Department of Justice did not name the "sham charity" in their press release.

The Al-Khair foundation maintains that Hasna is not an employee but works with one of its global partners to enable the delivery of aid around the world.

Hasna is being held following his arrest by the UK's National Crime Agency (NCA) and pending extradition proceedings before he can be taken to New York to face the US charges.

The US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York alleged Hasna used his senior role at a "purported global humanitarian organisation to coordinate directly with Hamas's senior leadership regarding the delivery of funds and supplies to Gaza, and the distribution of those funds and supplies at Hamas leadership's instructions".

Hasna is charged with conspiring to provide material support to Hamas, conspiring to finance terrorism and financing terrorism.

Each charge carries a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison, the US Department of Justice said.

US Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg said: "The money that flows from sham charities like the one described in the complaint fuels Hamas's terrorist activities, including the atrocities the group committed on October 7".

The Charity Commission said the Al-Khair Foundation recorded an income of more than Â£74m in the financial year ending 31 July 2025. The commission added it was made aware of the allegations against Hasna and "immediately started examining the serious concerns raised".

"The commission has now escalated its engagement to a statutory inquiry," the commission added.

Al-Khair is also subject to a legal order restricting some financial transactions being made without the consent of the Charity Commission.

News.title: Stray cats showing up at raves, gigs and pubs now have own merchandise
News.content:
Celebs pulling in punters with a club appearance is nothing new. But did they ever have so much fur?

At venues in Coventry at least, the glitterati wear whiskers these days.

It began when two stray cats made city venues their home, becoming social media stars thanks to the incongruous sights of tail and turntable, pint and paw.

While one shows up at gigs and rave nights, the other is a bit more pub than dub. But each now has his own range of merch... and visitors flock for a glimpse of these meeow-vers and shakers.

Murphy was first spotted living beneath a bush before wandering into the car park of The Old Windmill pub in the city centre, "rake thin" and in need of care.

Now a permanent resident, he has become a firm favourite with customers.

"We've had people who've never been in the pub before, but have seen him on social media," said the venue's Peter Dunkley. "They come in and the first question is 'where's Murphy'?"

Across town, Fargo is a well-known figure at Fargo Village, the creative hub after which he is named.

Regularly spotted around the site's shops and bars, he too has become an attraction in his own right, mixing among ravers and drinkers.

Fargo Village staff have set up an Instagram account in an effort to track down his owner, and it has attracted a loyal following of fans eager to keep up with his daily adventures.

News.title: Week-long celebration of Irish music and culture to come to a close
News.content:
From buskers on the bodhran to musicians firing up their fiddles, the atmosphere and the celebration of music and culture has been joyful.

Lots of people have been making the most of the open sessions, with chances to showcase their hidden talents, or learn new skills.

Visitors to the festival have been immersed in live music sessions, interactive workshops, dance classes and pop-up pubs for the past seven days.

The final day of the Fleadh will also be packed with performances at Belfast City Hall.

These include artists such as Ãirdan, Seoid, Celtic Roots and many more.

The closing ceremony will begin at 18:00 BST, kicking off with a performance from singer-songwriter and harpist Niamh Noade, and it will close at midnight with a performance from the winners of the Senior CÃ©ilÃ­ Band Competition.

More information can be found here., external

Aside from the performances at City Hall there will be a range of activities across the city centre.

The Seamus Heaney centre at Queen's University Belfast is hosting an exhibition, called Something to Say that looks at the personal and professional friendship between Seamus Heaney and David Hammond.

You can visit an Irish language craft and culture market at Conway Mill and there will be plenty of sessions, external going on with workshops and arts activities available.

News.title: Strictly dancers Ola and James Jordan separate after 23 years of marriage
News.content:
Former Strictly Come Dancing stars James and Ola Jordan have confirmed they have separated after more than 20 years of marriage.

The former professional dancers were regulars on the show for several series after first featuring in 2006.

The couple in a statement said they were "taking some time apart as we work through very difficult personal challenges".

"This has been an incredibly painful and emotional journey for us both and it certainly wasn't an easy decision," they said in a joint post shared on their Instagram accounts.

The couple said James had moved out the family home some time ago and they "don't know exactly what the future holds".

"Right now, more than anything we ask for kindness, empathy and a little privacy as we work through this as a family."

The couple's manager Vickie White had prevously said in a statement: "It is with great sadness that I can confirm that James and Ola began a trial separation some time ago

"Their shared priority remains co-parenting their daughter, Ella, and they are committed to putting her wellbeing first.

"They would greatly appreciate your understanding as they navigate this difficult time."

Ola Jordan won the Open Polish Championship in 1999 when she was 17 years old and became James' dance partner shortly afterwards in March 2000.

She moved to England a month later and the pair got married in October 2003.

James appeared on Strictly from 2006 to 2013 while Ola appeared on the show until 2015.

Ola's celebrity partners included wildlife presenter Steve Backshall and Welsh sprinter Iwan Thomas, while James danced with former international gymnast and broadcaster Gabby Logan, as well as The One Show presenter Alex Jones.

News.title: Hundreds flying out of Birmingham Airport left without luggage
News.content:
She described seeing a "build up" of luggage at the airport, after problems with the luggage belt, but had been assured by staff that it would be loaded on to the plane.

But on arrival at Dalaman they were told by the pilot that no bags had been loaded.

"We have heard nothing about compensation, no communication when our luggage is expected, we've heard nothing about who is liable for it. Is it the airport? Is it TUI? Is it our travel insurance? Who are we meant to go to? We've had nothing from anybody", Chapman said.

"It's just radio silence from the airport, apart from literally telling people 'we've got an issue'".

The first day of their holiday was spent travelling to a shopping centre to buy essentials for "for the next few days" but she added "we have no idea how long this is going to last".

"There are families all over the world at the moment with nothing and no idea of what's going on," she said.

"It's really important that Birmingham Airport are held accountable, and sort this out."

News.title: Simon Levy victims urged to come forward as police accused of 'litany of failures'
News.content:
Police have urged more victims of Simon Levy to come forward, as London's victims' commissioner said a "litany of failures" had allowed him to kill two women and rape a third.

Andrea Simon called for a review on the "failure to monitor him appropriately" when the 40-year-old was known to police as a sexual predator.

British Transport Police said women who recognised Levy as their attacker should report it, while the Met Police said it had investigated whether he had more victims, including further murders.

Meanwhile, the Independent Office of Police Conduct (IOPC) said a police constable is under investigation for gross misconduct, and a detective sergeant is facing a misconduct investigation.

On Friday, Levy was found guilty of murdering two women and raping a third in London while he was being monitored by the Met Police for being a convicted sex offender. He had previously committed a string of sex attacks.

The BBC reported how a series of grave failings by police, prosecutors and the courts left Levy free to murder, rape and sexually assault women.

Levy is due to be sentenced on Wednesday.

Former Strictly Come Dancing stars James and Ola Jordan have spoken out about the “difficult personal challenges” that led to their split.

It was announced on Saturday that the couple, who have been married since 2003 and share a six-year-old daughter named Ella, are “taking some time apart”.

Their manager, Vickie White, said that the pair “began a trial separation some time ago”.

The Jordans have now shared a joint statement, posted across both of their Instagram pages.

“We have always tried to be open and honest with the people who have supported us over the years and we feel it’s only right that this update comes from us,” they said.

“At the moment we’re taking some time apart as we work through very difficult personal challenges.”

open image in gallery Ola and James Jordan at Royal Ascot in 2018 ( Getty Images for Ascot )

The statement said that James “moved out of the family home some time ago”, and explained that their separation “wasn’t an easy decision”.

James, 48, and Ola, 43, are professional ballroom dancers and choreographers best known for their roles on Strictly.

The pair became household names after joining the show in 2006.

James featured on the show until 2013, partnering with stars such as Pamela Stephenson, Alex Jones, Denise Van Outen and Vanessa Feltz.

Ola competed on Strictly until 2015, where she danced with celebrities including DJ Spoony, Sid Owen, Steve Backshall and Iwan Thomas.

The Polish-born dancer also won the Glitterball trophy in 2009, partnered with TV personality Chris Hollins.

open image in gallery Ola and James have been together for 26 years and share a young daughter ( Getty )

James and Ola conceived Ella through IVF, and she was born in 2020 following a widely publicised three-year fertility struggle.

Their statement continued: “Our absolute priority, now and always, is our beautiful daughter Ella. She’s at the centre of everything we do.

“We are committed to co-parenting her with all the love, care and stability she deserves.”

It also discussed James’ mental wellbeing, saying he “hasn’t been in a good place for quite some time”.

“I’ve been struggling more than I’ve let people see and I’m taking the time I need to focus on getting myself to a healthier place, both for myself and for Ella,” it added.

The statement continued: “Neither of us is in a good place right now.

“We’re both doing our best to navigate one of the hardest chapters of our lives and we ask that people remember there are real people and real emotions behind every headline, every comment and every post.

“We don’t know exactly what the future holds. For now, we’re taking things one day at a time, doing what we both believe is best for ourselves, our family, and most importantly Ella.”

The message concluded by thanking their followers, fans and supporters for “the love, kindness and concern” that they have shown.

The couple also asked for “kindness, empathy and a little privacy as we work through this as a family”.

Actor and director Olivia Wilde has claimed that lucrative deals from streamers are tantamount to “bribes” to encourage film industry figures to forgo a cinema release.

Wilde, 42, directed and starred in The Invite, the acclaimed comedy about a couple who are navigating difficulties in their marriage, which are only made all the more clear when they invite their glamorous neighbours around for an impromptu dinner party.

She revealed how she fought for the movie, which also stars Seth Rogen, Penélope Cruz and Edward Norton, to be screened in cinemas rather than going straight to a streaming platform.

It’s a decision that has paid off, with The Invite going on to pass the $40 million (almost £30 million) mark at the box office globally, holding its own against much bigger budget blockbusters such as The Odyssey and the latest Spider-Man movie.

“They bribe you to not take theatrical [release],” Wilde told the press at the Locarno Film Festival. “We have to fight for it.”

open image in gallery Wilde appeared at the Locarno Film Festival to promote ‘The Invite’ ( AP )

“It’s a bribe,” she added. “They pay you more. Not the filmmaker, no. The financiers will get a lot more money to go to streaming, and you can take that bribe and give that up if that’s where your priorities lie.

“But we were really lucky that our financier gave me the opportunity to make this decision, which is something I don’t take lightly. She could have very easily said, ‘no, we’re going to go with a much bigger offer.’”

open image in gallery Olivia Wilde, Seth Rogan, Penelope Cruz and Edward Norton in 'The Invite' ( Film Nation )

“But I knew that she too felt this incredible reaction that happened at Sundance [film festival, where The Invite debuted], and that it was something worth investing in. We really believed that audiences deserve to discover this together.”

“I’m obviously really passionate about it but if I had been passionate about it alone, it wouldn’t have meant anything. I was passionate about it with a lot of support.”

The Invite is Wilde’s third feature film as a director, following 2022’s Don’t Worry Darling and 2019’s Booksmart.

“We’re constantly terrified by the sound of explosions. The electricity and water keep being cut off. We are without jobs and have no food. It feels like no one is coming to help the people of southern Iran. We don’t want war.”

These remarks reflect dozens of messages and first-hand accounts received by Independent Persian from residents of the southern provinces of Hormozgan, Bushehr, Khuzestan and Sistan and Baluchestan.

With intermittent US military strikes on southern Iran in recent weeks under a very precarious ceasefire, residents say they are now grappling not only with the threat of explosions but also prolonged power outages, water cuts, internet disruptions, shuttered businesses and a complete lack of meaningful government support.

One resident of Bandar Abbas tells Independent Persian that when the strikes came, the sound of explosions were almost uninterrupted throughout the night, prompting many families to sleep fully dressed with their identification documents nearby in case they needed to flee at a moment’s notice.

“Every morning the electricity is cut for two to four hours,” the local says. “When the power goes out, the air conditioning stops working, the water pumps shut down and we lose running water as well. In this heat, even a few minutes without air conditioning is unbearable, let alone several hours.”

open image in gallery An overturned car sits on a section of a destroyed bridge after a strike in Hormozgan province, southern Iran, July 18 ( AP Photo/Mahdi Negahban )

Not only do people live in fear of the airstrikes themselves but also the shockwaves from nearby explosions. Each blast raises concerns that windows will shatter and homes will be damaged. According to the resident, many people feel they have been left to fend for themselves.

Residents on Qeshm Island describe similar conditions. One resident says: “After all this anxiety and these explosions, the least we expected was for the water and electricity to keep running. Instead, the exact opposite has happened. The Islamic Republic welcomes war, but it cannot even provide people with the most basic services.”

The resident says that many families are now struggling to keep food and refrigerated medicines from spoiling, while repeated power fluctuations have damaged many household appliances.

A resident of Sirik adds: “Just last night my sister-in-law’s refrigerator burned out. We don’t have the money to buy her a new one that costs 500 million rials. Some of the explosions have been so powerful that windows have been blown out and walls and roofs have been damaged.

“People expected local officials or emergency services to check on residents after these incidents, but in most cases families cleared the debris themselves and relied on neighbours to help one another.

“When people go to government offices, either no one is there or they’re told to come back later. More than anything, people feel they’ve been forgotten.”

On Hengam Island, residents say their biggest concern – aside from the attacks – is the collapse of livelihoods tied to the sea. One resident explains: “Many families make their living from the sea. Fishing, passenger boats, tourism and traditional cargo vessels are the main sources of income.

“Now many people are too afraid to go out to sea and are effectively out of work. Tourists aren’t going to visit at a time of war. When fighting intensifies around the waters and ports, no one wants to risk their life. But if the boats don’t sail, families lose their income.”

open image in gallery Three boys play in the shallow waters of the Strait of Hormuz, as a plume of smoke rises from an explosion in the background, off Bandar Abbas, Iran, Monday, July 13 ( ISNA/AP )

Residents in Bushehr also reported experiencing explosions alongside power and water outages. One resident says: “It’s unbelievable that a province with so many refineries, power plants and energy facilities has to go for hours every day without electricity and water. We heard explosions at night, and during the day the air conditioners stop working.”

A resident of Jam tells Independent Persian that many government offices are either operating with skeleton staff or have shut down entirely. “If someone’s home is damaged or another problem arises, no one knows where to go for help.

“There doesn’t appear to be any plan to support affected families. It feels as though southern Lebanon is far more important to the authorities than southern Iran.”

In Chabahar, residents say they are facing not only security concerns but also a near-total halt or sharp downturn in economic activity. One resident says much of the local economy depends on the sea, with many families relying on fishing, maritime transport, ports and related industries for their livelihoods.

“When the ports are constantly being bombed, life comes to a standstill for us,” the resident adds. “Many people live on daily wages. If there’s no work, they have no money to support their families that day.”

Residents in Mahshahr and Sarbandar describe similar conditions. They say commercial activity at southern Iranian ports came to a complete halt following the renewed conflict and the US naval blockade, leaving thousands of families whose livelihoods depend on those ports facing severe financial hardship.

In Ahvaz, where temperatures are approaching 50 degrees Celsius (122°F), recurring power cuts and reduced water pressure remain among residents’ biggest concerns.

One resident says: “In this heat, a two-hour power outage makes homes unbearable. When the electricity goes out, either the water stops altogether or the pressure drops so much that it can’t reach upper floors without a pump. People in the south are worried about the explosions, the extreme heat, and losing both electricity and water. People have simply been pushed to their limit.”

open image in gallery People stand on a bridge destroyed after a strike in Hormozgan province, southern Iran ( AP )

Some of the messages received by Independent Persian also criticise government forces and members of the Basij militia, who before the latest round of fighting had publicly supported continuing the war and opposed negotiations.

One resident of Bandar Abbas writes: “Those who spent months in Tehran chanting slogans about war and resistance – where are they now? Why don’t they come to southern Iran and see the conditions people are living under?”

Another resident of Qeshm refers to the regime’s widely promoted “Jan Fada” (“Sacrifice Your Life”) campaign: “If there are really that many volunteers, why doesn’t at least some of them come to help the people of southern Iran? They don’t need to fight. They could simply help families whose homes have been damaged.”

The common thread running through most of the messages received by Independent Persian is a profound sense of abandonment. Residents say that as southern Iran faces military strikes, extreme heat, power outages, water shortages and an economic downturn simultaneously; their only real support comes from family members, neighbours and local communities.

Interviewees report that many government institutions have been largely absent or ineffective, reinforcing a widespread belief among residents that they are on their own.

Reviewed by Mohadese Tahery and Celine Assaf

Myanmar’s military-backed government has rejected the Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ (Asean) renewed call for the unconditional release of detained former leader Aung San Suu Kyi and dismissed the need for the organisation’s special envoy on Myanmar, according to the foreign affairs ministry.

President Min Aung Hlaing, the former army chief who had originally seized power in 2021 from Suu Kyi’s civilian government, has been trying to win political legitimacy since the takeover and resume relations with Asean.

Asean came up with a peace plan for the Southeast Asian country in April 2021 to end hostilities and initiate dialogue among contending parties, to be facilitated by the special envoy. Mr Min has since been barred from attending top-level meetings for failing to comply with the plan.

In an apparent effort to placate critics, the government allowed a representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross to visit 81-year-old Ms Suu Kyi last week, the first known contact with an outside international independent humanitarian organization since her detention five years ago.

Ms Suu Kyi is serving her sentence under house arrest at an undisclosed location in the capital Naypyitaw, on charges that her supporters and rights groups have said are politically motivated.

Myanmar's ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi, left, shakes hands with Arnaud de Baecque, resident representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross ( AP )

The current Asean chair, the Philippines, welcomed the meeting as a step toward dialogue and reconciliation on Friday, while urging greater access to political detainees and reiterating its call for Ms Suu Kyi’s “complete and unconditional release.”

Myanmar’s foreign ministry's statement late on Saturday criticised the call.

“Although the government has commuted her sentences based on humanitarian considerations, the matter of a full and unconditional release shall only be carried out in accordance with the law,” it said.

The statement also said the government will continue working with Asean’s current special envoy, Philippine foreign minister Maria Theresa Lazaro, but doesn’t see the need to continue down that path when Singapore takes over on 1 January, 2027.

“At present, the government, which emerged from the multiparty democratic elections reflecting the genuine will of the people, has assumed state responsibility,” the statement said.

In a speech more than three months after being sworn in as president following the elections, Mr Min dismissed Asean’s peace plan, saying some member states have discriminated against Myanmar and it would respond on a case-by-case basis.

Critics dismissed the elections, which were held in December and January, as a sham designed to consolidate the military’s grip on power while ostensibly restoring civilian rule.

The Red Arrows have been forced to pull out of a number of summer events in the UK after poor weather left them stranded in Canada.

The Royal Air Force (RAF) aerobatics display team are a popular fixture at air shows and military events around the country during the summer but they will not be able to fulfil three forthcoming engagements as their return across the Atlantic has been delayed.

They will not be performing at the Eastbourne International Airshow (13-16 August), the Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo (ongoing until 29 August) and Lyme Regis Lifeboat Week (15-22 August).

open image in gallery The Red Arrows are a fixture of summer air shows ( AFP/Getty )

The Red Arrows’ single-engine Hawk aircraft have a limited range and cannot carry out air-to-air refuelling, the RAF said.

As such, crossing the Atlantic has to be done in stages and requires having the correct RAF support aircraft, including search-and-rescue cover and those carrying essential technical equipment, in the right place, at the right time.

Weather in north-east Canada has been “particularly challenging”, the air force said, adding that the team will now have to begin its multi-leg journey back to the UK from next week.

Other RAF aircraft will participate at the events in the UK.

open image in gallery The RAF Red Arrows have had to pull out of a string of summer events ( PA )

The Typhoon Display Team and Battle of Britain Memorial Flight (BBMF) remain part of the line-up at Eastbourne.

The BBMF is also carrying out flypasts at Lyme Regis during Lifeboat Week, on 21 and 22 August.

A C-17 Globemaster and two Typhoon jets will now perform a flypast over the Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo on Saturday 15 August.

open image in gallery The Red Arrows perform a flypast over Windsor Castle during a state visit for US President Donald Trump on September 17, 2025 ( Getty )

The mayor of Lyme Regis Philip Evans, said he is “distraught” at the news that the Red Arrows have pulled out.

He added: “Lyme Regis Town Council had agreed to contribute £10,000 towards the overall cost of securing a visit by the Arrows and thanks to the generosity of the people Lyme and district, the full amount had been raised following the reforming of the Lyme Regis Red Arrows 100 Club.

“We will, of course, refund all the donations received.

“This is a particular disappointment for the RNLI as the Red Arrows display would have got this year’s Lifeboat Week off to a flying start.

open image in gallery The Red Arrows have been on tour in North America (file photo) ( PA Media )

“We will be going all out to try a secure a visit from the Arrows next year and I would like to thank the town council staff for all the hard work they have put in to rebuild the 40-year relationship between Lyme and the Red Arrows.”

A statement on the RAF website said: “The Red Arrows plan to continue a multi-leg journey back to the United Kingdom from North America next week (w/c 10 August).

“Due to a prolonged period of poor weather in the north-eastern regions of Canada, the team’s return from a tour of the United States was postponed last week.

“It is now anticipated this Atlantic crossing will be able to begin again from late next week based on more favourable conditions.

“Regrettably, this revised timeline means the Red Arrows will not be in a position to complete performances at Airbourne: Eastbourne International Airshow, the Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo and Lyme Regis Lifeboat Week.

open image in gallery The the Red Arrows fly over the Mall towards from Buckingham Palace following the armed forces procession on 5 May 2025 to celebrate the 80th anniversary of VE Day ( AFP/Getty )

“All of these events remain on as scheduled with exciting line-ups and featuring other participating RAF aircraft.

Wing commander Sasha Nash, officer commanding RAF Aerobatic Team, added: “We are very sorry the Red Arrows cannot participate at these events and we are grateful to organisers and communities for their understanding.

“Every effort is being made to ensure the Red Arrows can recommence the busy display season as soon as possible.

“However, safety is the only factor that will determine the timing of the team’s return from Canada.”
