Sports.title: How Joe Marler became an unlikely national treasure: Secrets behind rugby star's meteoric rise after Traitors fame - with Prince Harry appearing on his podcast - as he prepares for new Gladiators role
Sports.content:
How Joe Marler became an unlikely national treasure: Secrets behind rugby star's meteoric rise after Traitors fame - with Prince Harry appearing on his podcast - as he prepares for new Gladiators role

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Joe Marler spent most of his rugby career in the dirt, where mud, mauls and mayhem were at the very core of his identity.

But since hanging up his boots, the former England international has swapped scrums for studios, tackling for television and rucks for red carpets to become one the most popular stars of British mainstream media.

From building a successful podcast empire to appearing on a string of high-profile TV shows, Marler, 36, has carved out a new career that few could have predicted, becoming a familiar face far beyond the sport that made him famous initially.

It was announced on Monday that the powerful prop is set to become the first ever celebrity Gladiator when the fourth series of the BBC’s hit TV show returns in 2027, taking on the new identity of ‘Mauler’.

While appearing on Gladiators is not a huge departure from the physical and competitive world of England and Harlequins rugby, it was a very different BBC programme that transformed Marler from a cult figure among sports fans into a household name across the UK.

That popular TV show was Celebrity Traitors, where millions of viewers saw a side of Marler that had often been hidden beneath his rugged, intimidating and formidable appearance.

Joe Marler will be the first celebrity to appear as a Gladiator on the BBC's popular TV series

The former England rugby star has become a national treasure since his retirement

His appearance on the first series of Celebrity Traitors boosted his popularity away from sport

Away from the chaos and carnage of the rugby pitch was a self-deprecating and surprisingly vulnerable character who quickly became one of the breakout stars of the series.

His unlikely friendship with Ted Lasso actor and comedian Nick Mohammed became one of the show’s most memorable highlights, while his blunt observations and mischievous plotting made him a favourite among viewers who had never watched him play a single minute of rugby.

Yet Celebrity Traitors was not the beginning of Marler’s media career. By the time he stepped inside 'the castle', he had already spent years building a platform that would allow him to make the leap into mainstream media.

Rather than following the well-trodden path into rugby coaching or full-time punditry, the forward began cultivating a media career while he was still playing, launching The Joe Marler Show before evolving it into the hugely popular Things People Do podcast.

Co-hosted alongside sports journalist Tom Fordyce, the podcast deliberately avoided becoming another rugby chat show. Instead, Marler leaned into his natural curiosity and self-deprecating humour, eager to learn new perspectives from guests and share unique stories about his life so far.

Boxing promoter Eddie Hearn and Married at First Sight relationship expert Paul Brunson are among those to have joined Marler in the studio since, although the down-to-earth former rugby star continues to invite ordinary people with extraordinary jobs on to the show to share their stories and perspectives as well.

The success of the show opened the door to a second podcast, Joe Marler Will See You Now, which launched in the wake of his appearance on Celebrity Traitors and has quickly become extremely popular, sitting 19th in the charts currently.

Last month, listeners were left stunned when Prince Harry appeared as a guest on the show, adding to an impressive list of celebrities who have joined the ex-England prop on Joe Marler Will See You Now specifically, including Russell Howard, Dani Dyer, Joel Dommett, Joe Lycett, Prue Leith and Stephen Fry.

The rugby star chatted to Prince Harry on his popular Joe Marler Will See You Now podcast

The podcast currently sits 19th in the UK charts after Prince Harry's appearance last month

From raising £64,000 for CALM on Who Wants To Be A Millionaire? to featuring at Soccer Aid for UNICEF, Marler does done plenty of charity work after his retirement from rugby too

After proving his credentials behind the microphone, it wasn't long before TV producers came calling. Appearances on Michael McIntyre's The Wheel and Blankety Blank showcased just how comfortable Marler was on the small screen, while reports linking him with Celebrity Bake Off and the recent announcement of his Gladiators role suggest broadcasters increasingly see him as far more than simply a former rugby player.

Marler has never taken himself too seriously, either. During an appearance on Michael McIntyre's Big Show in January, he happily threw himself into a 'lip-sync battle' with RuPaul's Drag Race UK winner Blu Hydrangea, mouthing the words to Tina Turner's Simply the Best while dressed in a wig, skirt and glittery make-up.

His growing popularity has not gone unnoticed commercially too. Away from television, Marler has fronted campaigns for a string of popular brands, from Pringles and Sky Mobile to Jacamo and Sainsbury's.

Humour is often at the heart of these adverts, typified by Durex choosing Marler to front their tongue-in-cheek 'Fit Matters' campaign in July 2022. Filmed relaxing in a hot tub and discussing condom sizes with his trademark deadpan delivery, he played exactly the sort of self-deprecating, slightly absurd role that many former elite sportsmen might have avoided - but one that undoubtedly worked to his benefit.

Brand and Culture Expert Nick Ede believes his honesty and humour has been at the centre of his success post-retirement.

'His success comes from the fact that he has never tried to present himself as a polished media personality. Instead, he's leaned into being authentic, unpredictable and genuinely funny, and audiences have responded to that honesty,' he told Daily Mail Sport.

'What makes Joe so marketable is that he's incredibly relatable. He doesn't fit the traditional mould of the media-trained ex-professional athlete. He's happy to laugh at himself, talk openly about his struggles with mental health, poke fun at rugby culture and show the messy realities of life after elite sport.

'His retirement has actually given him more freedom to showcase that personality. Without the pressures and restrictions of being an active England international, he's been able to embrace opportunities across television, podcasts, radio and entertainment, allowing people who may never have watched a rugby match to discover him.

'His appearance on Celebrity Traitors was a pivotal moment because it introduced him to an entirely new audience who may have had little or no knowledge of his rugby career. Viewers saw his humour, strategic thinking and warmth, proving that his appeal extends well beyond the sporting world. That kind of mainstream exposure has significantly strengthened his profile and demonstrated that he has the charisma to succeed in entertainment as well as sport.

'He's also incredibly versatile. One minute he can be making audiences laugh on a panel show, the next he's having a thoughtful conversation about mental health or fatherhood. That range gives broadcasters confidence because they know he'll entertain while also bringing authenticity when a subject becomes more serious.

He was hailed a national treasure by Celebrity Traitors fans after his memorable appearances

'Brands are increasingly looking for ambassadors who can build trust rather than simply attract attention, and Joe ticks that box. He's imperfect, self-aware and refreshingly honest, which makes him highly credible.

'Consumers are far more likely to connect with someone who feels genuine than someone who appears overly polished, and Joe has built his reputation by never pretending to be anything other than himself.'

Fellow industry expert Rebecca May, Founder of RM Publicity, agreed: 'Joe is seen by audiences as entertaining - audiences see him as funny, quick-witted and honest - a combination that's incredibly likeable and marketable. Audiences respond to him, which is why he does so well on TV and continues to be booked.

'Just because an athlete or sportsperson has had a successful career and is well known doesn't mean that can translate into being a successful TV personality that audiences love. That is what separates Joe Marler apart - audiences automatically like him.

'I'd describe Joe's brand as controlled unpredictability. He’s fun, edgy and relatable but with enough spontaneity to keep people watching, which is why he is becoming a mainstream TV favourite.

'The audience is waiting to see what he says or does next, and that’s part his appeal. That balance is valuable in mainstream TV because it keeps viewers engaged.'

While refusing to take himself too seriously in terms of his public image, Marler has become an ambassador for multiple charities and mental health organisations since his retirement from rugby.

An ambassador for UK suicide prevention charity Campaign Against Living Miserably (CALM), Marler is passionate about breaking mental health stigmas and encouraging vulnerability among men, having raised £64,000 for the organisation during an appearance on Who Wants To Be A Millionaire? in 2024 and having starred in Sky's documentary Big Boys Don't Cry.

Marler also made his Soccer Aid debut for UNICEF earlier this year, lining up alongside the likes of Wayne Rooney, Jill Scott, Olly Murs and Robbie Williams. True to form, he stole the spotlight after being thrown on as an emergency goalkeeper, earning the fan-voted 'Moment of the Match' award for his unlikely cameo.

His wide-ranging interview with British GQ in February also showed how Marler's appeal has grown far beyond traditional sports audiences. The former prop discussed everything from retirement and fatherhood to mental health and finding purpose away from rugby, offering the same level of openness that has become a defining feature of his public persona.

It is that combination - the willingness to be both ridiculous and vulnerable - that has separated Marler from many former athletes attempting to build a profile after retirement. He has never tried to reinvent himself as a polished celebrity but instead has taken the same unpredictable personality that made him such a compelling rugby figure and simply moved it into a different arena.

Since walking away from rugby, he has become a reality TV star, podcast host, brand ambassador, mental health advocate and one of the most recognisable figures in British entertainment. Not bad for a 36-year-old who retired fully just two years ago.

A mischievous rogue and joker on the rugby pitch, Marler did not leave behind the personality that made him popular among sports fans. He simply used it to carve out another highly successful career.

Sports.title: Argentina rugby fans display 'Malvinas' banner laying claim to the Falkland Islands - as bad blood lingers after World Cup semi-final
Sports.content:
Argentina rugby fans display 'Malvinas' banner laying claim to the Falkland Islands - as bad blood lingers after World Cup semi-final

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Argentina continued to cause controversy around the Falkland Islands as fans of their rugby team held up a 'Malvinas' banner at their game against South Africa on Saturday.

During the match, which Argentina lost by a scoreline of 10-17, some supporters were seen with a sign that read: 'Los Malvinas son Argentinas', which translates to 'The Falkland Islands are Argentinian'.

The contention around the banner follows Argentina's World Cup semi-final victory over England at the FIFA World Cup.

After that triumph, their players used it as an opportunity to assert their claim over the Falkland Islands, a self-governing British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic Ocean located around 300 miles east of Argentina.

Britain have ruled the Falklands since January 1833 and in 2013 in a referendum, 99.8 per cent of citizens voted to remain as a British territory. The islands were the subject of a conflict between the two nations in 1982.

The lifting of the original banner - which also read 'Los Malvinas son Argentinas' - triggered a fierce backlash in the UK.

Argentina rugby fans held up a 'Malvinas' banner laying claim to the Falkland Islands

It came after their footballers did similar after beating England in the World Cup semi-final

Former Prime Minister Keir Starmer insisted that while 'the World Cup might not be ours, the Falkland Islands definitely are. Self-determination rests with the islanders and our commitment to the Falklands will never waver'.

FIFA subsequently opened an investigation, with the governing body's rules forbidding the use of any political messaging at the World Cup.

They had, however, previously turned a blind eye to continued references to the 1982 conflict in a song sung by the players – and posted on social media by the country’s association – in the dressing room throughout the tournament.

Argentina President Javier Milei described the players' celebration with the banner as 'perfectly valid,' and said the message 'reflects a sentiment shared by all Argentines'.

'I know that for Argentinians, we won the World Cup the moment we beat England because that's really what everyone wanted,' he said.

Tapia added: 'We are proud of our national teams' performance, and of the fact that they created that sense of epic invincibility - that nobody could beat us.'

The banner displayed on Saturday came in Argentina's first rugby game since their badly-tempered defeat by England last month, during which similar signs were displayed.

That was just a few days after the World Cup semi-final and the Pumas appeared to try to mock their rivals by wearing a kit paying homage to Diego Maradona's World Cup-winning 1986 team, a triumph made famous by Maradona's 'Hand of God' goal against England in the quarter-final.

Although England won that match, it ended in chaos when Argentina had a late try ruled out by the TMO, with their fly-half Tomas Albornoz subsequently suspended for four games for allegedly confronting the referee in fury.

Sports.title: Newcastle suffer pre-season injury scare as Anthony Elanga is carried off on a stretcher following horror challenge from Valencia star - but new boss Matthias Jaissle receives positive update on winger
Sports.content:
Newcastle suffer pre-season injury scare as Anthony Elanga is carried off on a stretcher following horror challenge from Valencia star - but new boss Matthias Jaissle receives positive update on winger

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Newcastle winger Anthony Elanga was stretchered off after a horror challenge that saw Valencia captain Jose Luis Gaya sent off during Saturday night’s friendly at the Mestalla Stadium.

The incident sparked a mass brawl after the home midfielder was given a straight red card for a high lunge that connected with Elanga’s shin just in front of the dugouts. The Swede was left writhing in agony on the turf while his team-mates emptied the bench and clashed with Valencia's players and staff.

Elanga received lengthy treatment to his right leg before a stretcher was called for, and he was clearly still in distress when he left the field. He had been Newcastle’s best player to that point and his loss was a sour end to the first half for new boss Matthias Jaissle, whose side trailed 1-0 at the interval.

However, the 24-year-old was able to walk in the dressing-room during half-time and it is thought he has avoided serious injury.

Sports.title: Tottenham star Jan Paul van Hecke hits out at Getafe's dirty tactics - and claims Spaniards could have had THREE red cards - in fiery training ground friendly
Sports.content:
Tottenham star Jan Paul van Hecke hits out at Getafe's dirty tactics - and claims Spaniards could have had THREE red cards - in fiery training ground friendly

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

An angered Jan Paul van Hecke hit out at Getafe's dirty tactics after Tottenham's clash with the Spanish side descended into a bruising affair.

Getafe are renowned for their rough-house approach and showed little sign of abating during the 70-minute encounter, which was played behind closed doors at Tottenham's training ground and proved anything but a routine pre-season friendly.

In one instance, Sandro Tonali, who joined Tottenham for £100million this summer from Newcastle, was left incensed by a challenge from Mario Martin. After Tonali had beaten Martin to the ball and shoved him to the turf, the Spaniard retaliated by leaving a leg in when Tonali attempted to play the ball forward.

Tonali was left furious, chasing after his opponent and grabbing his shoulder to turn him around before pushing him multiple times, including once to the neck.

Several Getafe players rushed towards Tonali and the approaching referee, while Andy Robertson stepped in to shove Kiko Femenia away as he attempted to complain to the official.

Centre-back Van Hecke, who joined Spurs from Brighton in a £52m deal this summer, said: 'Sometimes it's good to have a physical game. I thought today was a bit too much. From their side, sometimes it's not necessary, especially in a friendly.

'I think in a normal game maybe they have two or three red cards. But that's also maybe the way they play. We knew beforehand they can do it.

'It's a friendly, so you think maybe they would do it a bit less. But on the other hand, we also need to be at our best because if you don't put your foot in, they're going to win it.

🎥 Sandro Tonali scuffle in pre-season 🇮🇹 pic.twitter.com/XTGblesDyj — The Spurs Watch (@TheSpursWatch) August 8, 2026

Tonali was left incensed by a challenge from Getafe's Mario Martin, rushing up behind him and shoving him several times, including once to the neck

Several Getafe players rushed towards Tonali and the approaching referee after the incident

'If that's what the game asks, then you need to put your foot in and battle with them, otherwise they win the battles. That's what you don't want. It's one of the first things you need to win in football.

'You saw at times it got a bit heated, but that's because of the reactions. If you get kicked, you're going to react.'

As for the match itself, the goals were reserved for the final few minutes worth of action.

Getafe took the lead in the 66th minute when Alberto Risco volleyed past Spurs goalkeeper Antonin Kinsky.

Spurs then responded moments later with Conor Gallagher's neat finish following a good run drawing the game in the final minute.

The home side came close to clinching the match late on, with Richarlison's header saved by Getafe goalkeeper David Soria.

Both sides had chances in a goalless first half with Lucas Bergvall's shot the best of the efforts for Spurs, while Andy Gray did well to block Ebrahima Drammeh's drive.

De Zerbi made no changes through the 70 minutes played with barely a break at half time, with lots of senior players involved in another training game played at the training ground on Saturday. Six young subs were named plus goalkeeper Guglielmo Vicario. None were used.

Among those not involved against Getafe who are firmly back in the swing of preseason were Martin Dubravka, Kevin Danso, Micky van de Ven, Destiny Udogie, Rodrigo Bentancur, Pape Matar Sarr, Mateus Fernandes, James Maddison and Dominic Solanke.

Tottenham conclude their pre-season fixtures with a double header against Bundesliga side Hoffenheim next Saturday at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium (3pm UK) and a Sunday match at the training ground (12pm).

They begin their Premier League campaign against Brentford on 22 August.

Sports.title: Jose Mourinho lays into Bernardo Silva's fitness after Real Madrid debut - as he highlights how Man City legend 'doesn't do any work' while on holiday
Sports.content:
Jose Mourinho lays into Bernardo Silva's fitness after Real Madrid debut - as he highlights how Man City legend 'doesn't do any work' while on holiday

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Real Madrid boss Jose Mourinho has already hit out at Bernardo Silva after his debut for the club.

Mourinho returned to the Bernabeu earlier this summer, 13 years after his first spell, and one of his first targets was Man City legend Bernardo Silva.

The Portuguese midfielder was strongly linked with Barcelona and Atletico Madrid, but Real won the race and Mourinho wanted his captaincy experience and influence to help improve standards and behaviour in the dressing room following a trophyless season that spawned a number of divisive arguments.

After joining up with the squad later due to his participation with Portugal in the World Cup, Silva appeared for the first time in Saturday's pre-season friendly against Ferencvaros, yet Mourinho wasn't happy with what he saw.

'Bernardo Silva?' he said. 'He's a very important player for us. But the poor guy, when he goes on vacation, he likes to disconnect completely, he doesn't do any work.

'So he arrived for pre-season with much lower physical fitness, and he has to improve.'

Real Madrid boss Jose Mourinho hit out at Bernardo Silva's fitness after his debut for the club

Bernardo featured in Real's 2-1 win over Ferencvaros in pre-season in Budapest on Saturday

Despite his scathing criticism, the legendary Portuguese boss reserved some praise for the midfielder.

'But Bernardo is a wonderful player who gives us excellent build-up with the ball, whether he plays in a deeper position or in midfield (the 6 or 8 position),' he added.

'During the match I saw that he lacks physical strength, so I moved him to the 10 position. He can play there too. He can play in three or four positions.'

Mourinho's side ended up winning the clash 2-1 in what was their fourth pre-season friendly.

They face further matches against Deportivo and Schalke before kicking off the LaLiga season with a trip to Espanyol on August 22.

And Mourinho was happy with where his side were at, although he felt there were still areas for improvement.

He said: 'I liked the first half more. It doesn’t surprise me because we have been working more with those players. We had very good control of the game.

'In the second half, with Vini and Bernardo, who don’t have many minutes, and with Endrick changing positions, we lost some of our organisation. But it’s good.

'You don’t finish the game by giving away a dangerous free kick like we did. You have to know what to do. Those small mistakes that accumulate in these games are good for me.'

Mourinho did praise Bernardo's qualities but added that he has work to do on his fitness

Meanwhile, when departing City at the end of last season, an emotional Silva, who played 460 times for the club and broke down in tears on his final appearance, hailed his 'unbelievable' journey over nine years.

He said: 'It’s difficult because nine years, it’s a very long time. I would say that I leave as a Man City supporter.

'When I arrived from Portugal, I was a fan of Benfica, but now I can say that for sure that my feelings toward this club are very, very strong.

'I will be supporting Man City for the rest of my life. I also have the feeling of being grateful to the club, to the people, to what the fans gave me back. It was just unbelievable.'

Sports.title: Lionel Messi lands back in Rosario after father Jorge's death at 68... as Inter Miami teammate pays heartfelt tribute during game
Sports.content:
Lionel Messi lands back in Rosario after father Jorge's death at 68... as Inter Miami teammate pays heartfelt tribute during game

Lionel Messi has returned to his hometown of Rosario following the death of his father, Jorge.

Messi missed Inter Miami's Leagues Cup clash with Monterrey to fly back to Argentina where, according to reports in South America, the 39-year-old will attend a private memorial service.

Jorge Messi - who also served as his son's agent and business manager - died at the age of 68, two months on from the family revealing he had been rushed to hospital with an ongoing 'health situation'.

He reportedly passed away in a hospital in Rosario, close to the family home, at around 10pm local time on Friday August 7.

In the absence of their captain, Inter Miami players honored Jorge Messi by wearing black armbands, while fans paused for a moment of silence before kickoff. Earlier on Saturday, the team had posted a tribute which read: 'Our hearts are with our captain, Leo, and the entire Messi family.'

Against Monterrey, stand-in captain Rodrigo De Paul - Messi's international teammate - scored the opening goal and then pulled off his jersey to reveal another which read: 'Messi 10.' Unfortunately for Inter Miami, Monterrey scored late on to snatch a 2-1 win.

Lionel Messi has returned to his hometown of Rosario following the death of his father, Jorge

The soccer legend's father, pictured at the 2022 World Cup final, died at the age of 68

Rodrigo De Paul paid tribute to the Inter Miami captain during Saturday's clash with Monterrey

In the first official statement, Messi's first team Newell's Old Boys wrote in Spanish: 'Club Atletico Newell's Old Boys bids farewell with deep sorrow and grief to Jorge Messi, who passed away at the age of 68 in the city of Rosario.'

The club continued: 'Jorge was the pillar and the person who supported with vision, rigor, and affection the career of the greatest player of all time alongside his wife, Celia Cuccittini.

'His constant companionship and behind-the-scenes leadership were essential in backing every step of Lionel, from his beginnings at Malvinas to the pinnacle of world football glory. Thank you for teaching him to love these colors.'

Later on Saturday, both Barcelona and the Argentina national team added their own tributes.

'Stay strong, Leo Messi and family. We are with you in this difficult moment. We send you our most heartfelt embrace,' Argentina wrote on X.

A spokesperson for FC Barcelona, meanwhile, said in a statement: 'The President and the Board of Directors of FC Barcelona express their deepest condolences on the passing of Jorge Messi, the father of former Barca player and legend Lionel Messi, and, on behalf of the entire Barca family, extend their condolences to the Messi family.

'FC Barcelona thanks Jorge Messi for his commitment to our Club, for entrusting us with the beginnings and the most glorious years of his son Leo's football career. May he rest in peace.'

Sports.title: 'If we maximise everything, it's achievable': TOM CLEVERLEY on Plymouth's promotion charge, working 14-hour days and asking old friend Michael Carrick for help with signings
Sports.content:
'If we maximise everything, it's achievable': TOM CLEVERLEY on Plymouth's promotion charge, working 14-hour days and asking old friend Michael Carrick for help with signings

Unlock more of the best of our journalism with a DailyMail+ subscription - brilliant exclusives, in-depth insight and the writers you love every day

As a man who sang Stand By Me at his Aston Villa initiation in 2014, Tom Cleverley is grateful that Plymouth Argyle got the message more than a decade on.

He is preparing for a second campaign in charge of a club with which he has hit the depths – they were bottom of League One in late November – and very nearly the heights. That they only missed out on the play-offs in the dying minutes of last season is testament to his inspiration and resilience. That he was still in charge was down to the club's patience.

The target is still promotion this time around, but the Pilgrims' progress won't come easy when their competition includes Leicester City and Sheffield Wednesday. They have already sold star striker Lorent Tolaj for £4million to Bristol City and Cleverley will only get to spend some of that on a replacement.

But Cleverley knows his side can compete with the best in the division. Only Lincoln City had a better record in the third tier since the start of 2026 and the 36-year-old former Manchester United, England and Watford midfielder is more prepared than he was 12 months ago.

'I’ve learned a lot,' he tells Daily Mail Sport. 'The biggest thing is my knowledge of League One. I researched every player we were playing against but until you’ve experienced the heat of the battle, it’s tough to know how to be at your most effective. You never stop learning. You want to be in the training ground 14 hours a day but you quickly learn that's got a short shelf life.

'I've got to grips with what the league takes. I know the strengths and weaknesses of my players. If we maximise every department of the football club, promotion is achievable.

Tom Cleverley is preparing for his second campaign in charge of Plymouth Argyle

He has struck up a strong relationship with supporters after a fantastic run of form in 2026

'I'm very detailed. Which side you press someone off, to when you’re pressing, are you checking your shoulders? All these things, really tactical. Be detailed to give your players an edge, but don't overload them.

'I wouldn’t pigeonhole myself into one style of tactical identity. I’m someone who believes in getting the best out of the players you’ve got, identifying their strengths and weaknesses, and creating a gameplan.'

Cleverley cites Unai Emery as one manager he admires for his adaptability, detail and record of improving players. In the Football League, when bigger clubs regularly poach players, being able to work with what you've got is vital.

He has also called in a few favours from an old Manchester United team-mate, with whom he won a Premier League title in 2013. Michael Carrick let Plymouth train at United's Carrington base last season before their trip to Stockport County.

'We’ve used Carrington, so I see Jonny Evans and Michael there,' Cleverley says. 'We’re good friends away from football, so we've had real good conversations about potential loans. Every young English coach will be rooting for him this year.'

Cleverley enjoys listening to Oasis, Blossoms and Courteeners, all bands from his old city. He'll certainly need some music for the season ahead, when he will spend more than 12,000 on coach trips with his squad for away days from Devon.

Plymouth were surprisingly strong on the road last campaign. They earned 39 points on their travels (one fewer than when they won the title in 2022-23), winning 12 games.

Typically, they travel the morning before a match and train at a club's facilities nearby, before getting home as late as 4am on the night of the game. Players then get a day and a half off to recuperate.

'I've got to grips with what the league takes. I know the strengths and weaknesses of my players. If we maximise every department of the football club, promotion is achievable'

Cleverley (left) with Michael Carrick (right) in the 2012-13 season, when they won the Premier League together in Sir Alex Ferguson's final season in charge

'You want to be in the training ground 14 hours a day but you quickly learn that's got a short shelf life'

'The travelling isn't mentioned as much internally as it is externally!' says Cleverley. 'We try to recruit the right profile of player and character that doesn’t moan about small things.

'We know what we’re signing up for here. We do have the challenge of miles on the clock. It’s not a negative or an excuse, it’s a challenge, and we come across challenges big or small every day.'

After being the first person in and last person out every day, Cleverley is feeling 'refreshed' after a few weeks back home in Manchester and on holiday in North Wales this summer. He's also been to St George's Park to work on his English Pro Licence.

His more than 400 games as a player and manager have contained immense highs and lows. Roy Hodgson once compared him to Cesc Fabregas and he picked up 13 caps for England. He was also relegated with Watford and was the subject of a fan petition to exclude him from the 2014 World Cup, which hit the then 24-year-old hard.

All of that has given him a certain detachment when it comes to the struggles of football. In the pressure cooker of last October and November, when he looked on the brink of losing his job, Cleverley didn't flinch.

'It wasn’t as difficult as some people might have thought,' he says. I suffered a very difficult time in my playing career when I was 23, 24, that gave you a numbness and a thickness of skin in your life.

'It’s difficult not seeing your team win because you don’t sacrifice your life for poor performances or results. That’s hard. You sacrifice so much to see no outcome. But the abuse, I can take that, I've been in football long enough. I enjoy being the person to give direction out of those moments.'

Cleverley's emotional stability is just as well, because he intends to be in this for the long haul. He has embraced the Plymouth community and sees his job as a project.

Roy Hodgson once compared Cleverley (right) to Cesc Fabregas (centre)

He won 13 caps for England and represented Team GB at the London 2012 Olympics

Cleverley's emotional stability is just as well, because he intends to be in this for the long haul. He has embraced the Plymouth community and sees his job as a project

After arriving in Devon, Daily Mail Sport has learned, he went on a local history tour to understand the city. As we speak, he is celebrating a £65,000 grant from Sky Bet for Plymouth to run a programme helping women through their perimenopause and menopause.

'We’re a club that really does walk the walk when we say we’re a community club and a family club,' he says. 'We have days with open training, Christmas carols, whatever it may be, we try to engage and give back to our loyal supporters.

'I’m certainly passionate, intense, players will call me quite detailed. I want to create an energy within the stadium. That’s a real important connection. I’m excited to be on this journey.'

Tom Cleverley was speaking after Plymouth Argyle received a £65,000 grant from the Sky Bet EFL Building Foundations Fund to launch a new programme supporting women through perimenopause and menopause.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat

World Cup play-off finals - Europe Bosnia & Herzegovina vs Italy

Sweden vs Poland

Kosovo vs Turkey

Czech Republic vs Denmark

How Ireland threw away their lead

Ireland came flying out the blocks flying in Prague. Four shots in the opening ten minutes, including Nathan Collins crashing a shot off the bar from range, set the tone for a brilliant display - and they got their rewards.

A long throw caused chaos and Nathan Collins was deemed to have been caught slightly late by Vladimir Darida by VAR, who sent referee Glenn Byberg to the monitor for a review.

Troy Parrott, who else, crashed in the penalty for his sixth goal in the last three Ireland matches. And it got better for Ireland four minutes later.

Ryan Manning's corner found Dara O'Shea at the back post and his header across was cleared off the line by Vladimir Coufal - but off goalkeeper Matej Kovar and over the line.

Image: Czech Republic goalkeeper Matej Kovar scores an own goal to give Ireland a 2-0 lead

Ireland were in dreamland but a moment of Manning madness brought the Czech Republic back into it. The defender's needless tug back on Krekci - when the ball was heading out of play - was penalised by referee Byberg, with Patrick Schick pulling one back from the spot.

Ireland did, however, manage to settle the nerves down - right throughout the second half. Despite sustained Czech pressure in the second half, they barely threatened.

It was Ireland who had the better chances after the break, with Jayson Molumby striking the post and Parrott denied by a solid Kovar save at a corner. But then heartbreak struck with four minutes of normal time remaining, as Krejci bundled the ball in at the near post from a set piece.

Krejci could have even won it with the last kick of the game but scuffed his finish, as extra-time came.

Substitute Tomas Soucek missed a glorious chance for the hosts, with Adam Idah was denied a one-on-one chance by a goal-saving challenge from Stepan Chaloupek. Penalties came and the lottery fell in the hosts' favour.

Image: Jan Kliment scored the winning goal in the penalty shoot-out

Hallgrimsson confident in Ireland future despite 'pain'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"One word is pain. I feel pain. I feel pride for the performance of the players. They gave it all. I feel gratitude for all the supporters who supported us through the whole game, even after the loss. I feel pride being a part of that group. Personally, I know all the players will feel pain now. Only pain.

"We take with us that we can play teams higher in the FIFA ranking and can punch above our weight: Portugal, Hungary and here. We can compete with these teams. We came here with three wins in a row, a long time since that happened for this national team.

"So there's growth in this squad. It's maturing. These are been the biggest game most of these players have played. That's encouraging to know we're growing. It's strange to say that after we lost today.

"I know I'm biased in this, all the statistics and metrics of the team have improved. Big games, being on the line, crunch times all the time, we've managed to go through this. It showed the resilience, character of these players, that's why I feel confident going on."

Sports.title: Wilson key for Wales, NI aim for big upset while history beckons for ROI
Sports.content:
Sky Sports assesses Thursday's 2026 World Cup play-off semi-finals as Wales host Bosnia-Herzegovina, Northern Ireland go to four-time winners Italy and the Republic of Ireland face Czech Republic in Prague.

Thursday 7.45pm: Wales vs Bosnia-Herzegovina (winner will play Italy or Northern Ireland)

Harry Wilson is not the new Gareth Bale, but he's doing the job of Bale at his best, especially for Wales.

Fans have long been excited about Wilson's natural talent, but are now seeing his influence in the Premier League on a weekly basis for Fulham. This season, he has 10 goals and six assists for club, while for country, his stats are even better with five goals and two assists in his last five games.

If Wilson starts running the show, his confidence will feed to the other players and to the home crowd, and Wales will be very difficult to stop on their own patch.

Which World Cup group would Wales be in? If Wales qualify for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Craig Bellamy wanted to create an identity for Wales when he took over as head coach. It's now clear: he wants front-foot football coupled with intensity and energy.

Bellamy doesn't always see that in international football as he finds it slower at times compared with club football, but his Wales side will not be ponderous. You could see during the qualification campaign that Wales' intensity in winning the ball back very quickly and holding possession grew. Now it's about consistently doing it.

Apart from consistency in play, there needs to be consistency in selection. Much is always made about the 'spine' of a good team, from the goalkeeper to the glory hunter! Leeds United provide a fair chunk of Wales' spine with 'keeper Karl Darlow on form and in receipt of the No.1 keeper's jersey. Joe Rodon is the rock at centre-back that success relies upon, while team-mate Ethan Ampadu's versatility means he can link anywhere between defence and midfield. Throw in one of the in-form Premier League stars, Harry Wilson, and a strong spine can take a team a long way.

Ask Bellamy if he has thought about preparing for the play-off final against either Italy or Northern Ireland and you'll get glared at. It's Bosnia, Bosnia and Bosnia. He won't entertain anything beyond Bosnia until the game is over. It's a danger, a banana skin he wants to avoid. Thinking too far ahead isn't good on this occasion.

Geraint Hughes

Thursday 7.45pm: Italy vs Northern Ireland (winner will play Wales or Bosnia-Herzegovina)

On paper, perhaps in reality, it's David vs Goliath.

Northern Ireland enjoy David vs Goliath. Once upon a time it was David (Healy) vs England and David (Healy) vs Spain.

For smaller nations there is comfort in being the underdog. A loss would be met without a major backlash, a win makes you a hero. That's how Michael O'Neill's side will approach Thursday's assignment in Bergamo against Italy.

Which World Cup group would Northern Ireland be in? If Northern Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Conor Bradley and Daniel Ballard are out. Between them they represent 50 per cent of the Northern Ireland players currently plying their trade in the Premier League.

The pair's absence is as much a blow to Northern Ireland's attacking prospects as it is defensively. Ballard represents their best aerial threat from set-pieces, Bradley their most dynamic player on the ball.

And yet for some reason that only football can explain, hope remains. The four-time World Cup winners are heavy favourites but far from the Azzurri powerhouse of old.

If Northern Ireland have it their way, it's unlikely to be a pretty spectacle. But can they frustrate their hosts? 0-0 at half-time? Pounce on the sense of angst that will exist among the home support?

To call it a free hit would be to downplay the importance of the game. But Northern Ireland are free from the weight of expectation.

Daring to dream of a result that becomes instant folklore.

Michael Morrow

Thursday 7.45pm: Czech Republic vs Republic of Ireland (winner will play Denmark or North Macedonia)

Image: Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson and captain Seamus Coleman spoke to the media in Prague

History beckons for the Republic of Ireland here in Prague.

Make no mistake, this will be the biggest game to date for a lot of these Irish players as they attempt to take another step to this summer's World Cup but they must get past Czech Republic to do so.

Which World Cup group would Republic of Ireland be in? If the Republic of Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group A with co-hosts Mexico, South Africa and South Korea.

Still coming off the euphoria of the incredible back-to-back wins against Portugal and Hungary last November, this is an Irish team full of confidence.

Having spoken to a few people around the Czech Republic team, those results have been noted and they are particularly worried about Irish striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in those two games in November - including the 96th-minute winner against Hungary.

Head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson spoke ahead of this game about one of the key aspects is visually and mentally being ready for the challenge ahead of them, he seemed as calm and confident as usual.

However his key selection dilemma is does he bring back the experienced, tried and tested players such as Seamus Coleman, Robbie Brady and Chiedoze Ogbene - all three have had limited game-time this season for a variety of injuries.

Coleman and Brady especially are the only two players in the squad who were part of Ireland's last team in a major tournament which was in 2016 - their experience could prove vital.

Image: Can Troy Parrott recreate his Irish heroics in Prague on Thursday?

Their opponents are in a state of flux.

Czech Republic have a new head coach who takes charge of his first game on Thursday, with West Ham's Tomas Soucek also being stripped of the captaincy after November's internationals having caused shockwaves in the local media - Wolves' Ladislav Krejci has replaced him.

The pressure feels like it's all on the home side which could play into Ireland's advantage as they look to take another step to qualify for this summer's World Cup - their first since 2002.

Danyal Khan

Semi-final: Wales vs Bosnia and Herzegovina

Final: Wales/Bosnia and Herzegovina vs Italy/Northern Ireland - Tuesday, 7.45pm kick-off

Final: Slovakia/Kosovo vs Turkey/Romania
