World.title: Jamaica’s Edwards snatches triple jump gold at World U20 Champs
World.content:
In this March 2026 file photo, Jamaica College star Michael-Andre Edwards displays his gold medal after winning the Class 1 Boys’ triple jump final, with a leap of 16.25m., to close out his Champs career. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

OREGON, USA – Michael Andre Edwards thought he would be able to jump “about 16.80m” but surprised himself with a dramatic final round 17.08m (1.1m/s) leap to snatch the gold medal at the World Athletics Under- 20 Championships at Hayward Field in Eugene, Oregon.

Edwards, who started slowly, trailed his good friend American Miles Nesmith going into the final round, when he produced the jump of his life on the biggest stage.

After his dramatic win, he said he never expected he would be jumping this far this soon but never thought 17.00m was out of his reach.

He twice bettered his previous personal best of 16.30m set in July, with 16.71m in the fifth round and then his big jump a round later. He joins national under-20 record holder Jaydon Hibbert,17.87m, and James Beckford, 17.29m, as the only Jamaican juniors to jump over 17.00m in the triple jump.

Edwards is also the second Jamaican man to win the triple jump after Hibbert won it in 2022.

This was Jamaica’s first gold of the champions and third medal after Gary Card and Shanoya Douglas won silver medals in their respective 100m finals on Thursday.

Nesmith, who was second to Edwards at the Penn Relays in April, took the silver medal with a personal best 16.79m (1.0m/s) and China’s Zhuoyue Wang was third with 16.36m (0.9m/s).

Edwards, who needed just one jump, 16.00m, to qualify from the prelims, started slowly with a 13.76m (1.4m/s) but qualified for the final with a 16.23m (-0.3m/s) in the third round before he got into second place with 16.71 (0.5m/s) in the fifth round.

-Paul A Reid

World.title: Hurting Jamaica
World.content:
An inflatable obstacle course at the entry fee-free Harmony Beach Park in Montego Bay, St James.

FALMOUTH, Trelawny — Minister of Tourism Edmund Bartlett has criticised people who he says are creating a false impression internationally that Jamaicans are being denied access to the country’s beaches.

Speaking at the 2026 Artisan Village Food Festival in Falmouth on Thursday, Bartlett argued that the facts do not support the narrative being circulated overseas and the false claims are damaging Jamaica’s reputation and costing the Government money to correct.

“We have 70 [public bathing beaches] in Jamaica, all around the island. And of that 70 only 10 of them are paid beaches. And then only five of that you would pay a decent money to go to,” Bartlett said.

“And yet, some of us, when you hear what we say to the international media… you would believe that every beach in Jamaica is just locked off, and that’s not fair to Jamaica. That’s not fair to us,” added Bartlett.

He argued that concerns may arise about access to specific beaches, but insisted that isolated issues should not be used to broad-brush the country.

“So we say, if you have an issue with one, or two, all right, let’s talk about that. Let’s deal with it because everywhere in the world you go, there’s an issue. But we must deal with it and resolve it, and not define ourselves by it,” argued Bartlett.

The tourism minister said the Government has had to invest in advertising and promotional campaigns to counter misinformation in the international media.

“You know as minister of tourism how much trouble I get on international press to go and explain to them that it is not true? Then we have to spend money with advertising agents… to tell them seh nothing nuh go so,” Bartlett said.

He urged Jamaicans to resolve national challenges internally rather than tarnishing the country’s image overseas.

“So we have to help ourselves. Where we have a problem, let us resolve it. Let us see where the difficulties are, talk about it, deal with it at home, solve it at home. And, as Miss Lou seh, ‘Don’t wash your dirty linen abroad,’ because when you believe you are hurting your neighbour, you’re not hurting your neighbour, you’re hurting your country and, in the end, yourself,” Bartlett added.

He lamented what he described as a tendency among some Jamaicans to highlight only the country’s shortcomings.

“Some of us enjoy beating up little Jamaica. Some of us enjoy saying all the negative things about the country, and some people I hear say things like Jamaica refuse to make its people enjoy the beaches. I never hear anything like that,” he said.

Bartlett urged Jamaicans to use the country’s 64th anniversary of Independence to embrace a new conversation and project a more positive image of the nation.

“And as we do that, the second thing I want to concern my mind and to get you into my thoughts on is how it is that we project ourselves as a people and as a country,” Bartlett said.

“The world views us through our own eyes and through our prisms. The world sees us the way we see ourselves, but most importantly, the way we express who we are to the world,” he added.

Bartlett said Jamaica’s 64th Independence anniversary should mark the beginning of a more positive national outlook.

“So, on this 64th birthday, let us resolve to have a new conversation, a new narrative, a positive contribution to ourselves, as together we grow. As we recover from Melissa, we recover stronger and better, and we build this great little piece of rock. In the words of Miss Lou, ‘We little but we tallawah,’” he said.

Official data show Jamaica possesses approximately 1,022 kilometres of coastline, of which approximately 29 per cent (300 kilometres) consists of sandy beaches.

World.title: Germany battling “daily” hybrid warfare attacks, minister warns
World.content:
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt speaks to the media during a news conference at Leipzig Airport on August 5, 2026. | Jens Schlueter/Getty Images

Last week’s drone incident in Lepizig just the latest example.

Germany is being hit by hybrid warfare attacks from foreign powers on a “daily” basis, the country’s interior minister has warned, after a drone packed with explosives was found at Leipzig Airport earlier this week.

Espionage, sabotage, cyber attacks and covert actions “with the aim of destabilizing Germany or directly harming it” are a “constant reality,” German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told BILD in an interview on Sunday.

Dobrindt suggested on Thursday that a drone incident at Leipzig Airport may have been an attack by a state actor. The minister has stopped short of specifying which foreign powers are behind the hybrid attacks.

World.title: Magyar’s party backs former supreme court head for Hungarian president
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s ruling Tisza party said on Saturday that it had nominated former Supreme Court President András Baka to become the country’s next president.

Baka, who worked as a judge on the European Court of Human Rights before being elected to head the Supreme Court, was removed from his post by the Fidesz government in 2011 — a move the ECHR ruled was unlawful.

“Throughout his career, Dr. András Baka has considered the principle of the separation of powers to be of paramount importance and has consistently stood up for the rule of law and judicial independence,” Tisza said in a Facebook post.

Spanish authorities and the European Commission this week confirmed that none of the 72,000 people who surged into Ceuta have crossed the Strait of Gibraltar. During a meeting of EU interior ministers on Tuesday, Italian Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi publicly praised Spain for its handling of the situation and expressed Rome’s “sincere solidarity” with Madrid.

Yet despite requests from Madrid, the Italian government has declined to end border checks even after it became clear that there was no risk of the Ceuta crisis spilling into the rest of Europe. Rome’s inaction prompted Spain to issue a statement on Friday threatening to adopt “proportional measures” if Rome did not change course by Aug. 9.

After Meloni’s office responded by declaring “Italy does not accept ultimatums or demands from abroad regarding national security and border control,” Madrid moved to reintroduce its own controls.

Magnus Brunner, the European commissioner for internal affairs and migration, sought to mediate in the dispute.

“I was in contact with both the Spanish and Italian Interior Ministers today. Both confirmed that the internal border controls are temporary,” Brunner said in a post on X. “I stressed the progress we’ve made on tackling illegal migration and that trust between Member States is our most valuable currency.”

World.title: Gabriel Attal alleges Russian interference in French presidential race
World.content:
Gabriel Attal attends a session of questions to the government at the National Assembly, in Paris on January 6, 2026. | Christophe Petit Tesson/EPA

Attal becomes the latest contender to file a complaint over alleged Russian interference ahead of the April 2027 presidential vote.

Former prime minister and presidential candidate Gabriel Attal has filed a complaint over an alleged Russian disinformation campaign ahead of next year’s French presidential election, local news outlets reported on Saturday.

Attal’s lawyers told French media that the complaint, filed on Friday, denounces “acts of foreign interference, manipulation of information, fabrication of content likely to undermine the fundamental interests of the nation and the sincerity of the upcoming presidential election.”

They told BFMTV that several accounts on social network X, some of which impersonated French and international media, had disseminated fake video reports and newspaper articles attributing false statements to Attal that were “intended to discredit him as a candidate.”

World.title: Germany’s gas gamble puts Europe’s winter at risk
World.content:
The low reserves have already added to the increased pressure on gas prices linked to renewed tensions around the Strait of Hormuz, with the European natural gas benchmark now consistently higher than it was for the first four months of the Iran war.

The European Commission, the EU’s executive arm, has said the bloc faces no winter supply risks. But a report by energy analytics firm Rapidan projects that reserves will rise to only 65 percent of total storage capacity by November, arguing that hitting the EU's target by winter won't be possible without "materially higher prices."

That risk has been exacerbated, analysts say, by the bloc’s move in recent years to replace its long-term supply deals with Russia with short-term purchases of globally traded liquefied natural gas. These seaborne cargoes are highly mobile and go to the highest bidder — leaving buyers more exposed to volatility on international markets, especially in the wake of the loss of key supplies from Qatar and rising demand in Asia.

A tanker passes through the Strait of Hormuz on Feb. 25, 2026. | Fadel Senna/AFP via Getty Images

Germany, the bloc's largest gas consumer, has seen its reserves fill up even more slowly than others, in part thanks to its more hands-off, market-led approach to restocking than many of its neighbors. As a result, reserves stood at only 47 percent of national capacity in August, according to the latest data — the lowest fill level since records began. That's especially worrying as the country's reserves are important for the bloc as a whole, representing over 20 percent of the EU's storage capacity.

Nevertheless, Berlin is staying the course. While its energy ministry has acknowledged the country's historically low reserves, it has refused to intervene to direct its main state-controlled gas buyers, SEFE and Uniper, to buy gas at current prices to ensure its targets are met, instead of waiting for market conditions to improve.

"It is the responsibility of companies and traders to fill the storage facilities for the winter," a spokesperson for the German energy ministry told POLITICO. "Government-led filling of the storage facilities would further constrain the gas market and drive prices even higher. The supply situation over the coming months would actually deteriorate."

World.title: Roman shipwreck with hundreds of amphorae found off Sicily
World.content:
Extraordinary discovery off the coast of Sicily. A Roman-era shipwreck, probably dating from between the 2nd and 1st centuries BC, has been located around three miles off the coast of Mazara del Vallo, at a depth of 46 metres.

 

On the seabed, the Italian Ministry of Culture reports, there are hundreds of amphorae, mostly of the Dressel 1A type, two lead anchor stocks and another structure made of the same material.

The Minister for Culture, Alessandro Giuli, has described it as one of the most important underwater archaeological discoveries of recent years. "I congratulate the Carabinieri, their specialised units and the Sea Superintendency of the Sicilian Region for the expertise and dedication that made this result possible. The sea continues to give back precious fragments of our history and the wreck of Mazara del Vallo tells us about the people, the routes and the trade that made the Mediterranean a crossroads of civilisations. Research will continue to uncover its story and share it with the public," Giuli said.

The discovery was made during a joint inspection carried out by the Carabinieri Cultural Heritage Protection Unit (TPC) in Palermo, the Sea Superintendency of the Sicilian Region and the Carabinieri Underwater Unit in Messina, with support from the Carabinieri patrol boat in Trapani, following a tip-off from private citizens.

Remains of the Roman wreck found off Mazara del Vallo Ministero della Cultura italiano

The site will now be the focus of further documentation and research by the Sea Superintendency, aimed at reconstructing the archaeological context and putting in place the necessary protection measures.

The volcano discovered off Panarea

Only a few days ago another major discovery off Sicily was announced. In this case, however, it was not an archaeological find. A large crater hidden beneath the sea and new hydrothermal vents were identified off the island of Panarea, in the Aeolian archipelago. The discovery will allow scientists to deepen their study of the island's submarine volcanic system and raises new questions about its evolution.

The structure lies about one nautical mile north-east of Panarea, at a depth of between 60 and 80 metres. The crater is of impressive size: about 100 metres long and 60 metres wide. Next to this formation, new hydrothermal vents have also been identified, characterised by gas emissions from the seabed.

World.title: 14,000 UFO sightings in Germany: reporting centre in Hesse investigates
World.content:
The Central Research Network for Extraordinary Celestial Phenomena (CENAP) is a point of contact for people in Germany who are looking for a scientific explanation for what they observe in the sky.

 

CENAP director Hansjürgen Köhler says they have never received as many reports as they do at the moment: "We receive between three and six reports a day. Without question, we're the busiest reporting centre in the German-speaking world." By August 2026 he and his team had cleared up some 14,000 cases.

Köhler is an amateur astronomer; it all started "with youthful recklessness."

"We were working at the observatory and expanding our knowledge there. Back then, lots of calls were coming in and the observatory was getting fed up with it. That prompted us to take a closer look at the whole UFO subject."

As an 11-year-old he watched the moon landing on television. It left a deep impression on him and laid the foundations for his interest. "If I'd known back then what was coming, I wouldn't have done it; there really were a few annoying years, but these days I enjoy it because we can give people a sensible explanation."

"In 1973, at the beginning, when we were young men starting to grapple with this subject, we obtained microfilms from the USA from the Second World War era showing flying objects that were considered inexplicable phenomena."

"We realised that even back then, during the war, there were repeated natural phenomena," says Köhler. "Some of the images were quite striking – not least because of the pilots' reactions, as they asked themselves in astonishment what might just have flown past them."

Pentagon files put UFOs back in the spotlight

Today, with the Pentagon in Washington having released the so-called UFO files, the topic is gaining momentum again.

After the US Navy had already released videos showing unidentified flying objects – now officially mostly referred to as "Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena" (UAP) – the Pentagon in April 2020 for the first time formally confirmed the authenticity of three recordings from 2004 and 2015. The videos show encounters between US military pilots and flying objects whose origin could not initially be clearly determined.

In December 2022 the "All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office" (AARO) was even set up within the US Department of Defense. The office is tasked with systematically investigating UAP reports, assessing any potential threats to national security and reviewing past cases.

For Köhler, that's old hat: "We already know the archives anyway; there was nothing in them that was new to me. For the younger generation, though, it is something new. We can only yawn when we see the old footage."

One of the recordings, the so-called "Gimbal" video, was made in January 2015 during a training flight by a US Navy F/A-18 off the coast of California. The infrared footage shows an unidentified object that appears to rotate on its own axis and is commented on in astonishment by the pilots. The Pentagon itself has confirmed the authenticity of the recording but, by its own account, has so far been unable to clearly establish the object's exact identity.

Köhler is convinced that the video shows nothing more than a balloon. He explains its apparently rapid movement as a relative motion between the aircraft and the balloon: because of the jet's high speed, it creates the impression that the object is racing past at enormous pace.

He also has something to add on the F/A-18 itself: "Ever since it was introduced by the US Navy it has had issues with its electronic tracking systems. It has received nine updates to get that under control, and there are still misreadings, including in the speed indications."

But, as Köhler says with some frustration, "all of that simply gets lost. The film is shown again and again, and the debunking is like a drop in the ocean, it too just disappears. Above all on social media and on X, the kind of tall tales that are told there are so absurd. I don't even watch it any more because it annoys me; it runs counter to my work."

I do not deny that there is life out there. Hansjürgen Köhler Founder of Germany's only UFO reporting centre CENAP

Köhler boils down the reports that reach him to one core idea: "Supposedly, visitors from far out there drop by every day to see what we're up to here. I do not deny that there is life out there. But are we really to believe that they travel across galaxies with highly advanced technology to our blue planet and then crash of all places here above the desert?"

Critics of CENAP occasionally complain that the organisation assesses many UFO sightings very sceptically and places a strong emphasis on conventional explanations. Supporters see that as precisely the organisation's strength: CENAP seeks to classify observations in scientific terms and distinguish between genuinely unexplained phenomena and misinterpretations.

The differing assessments mainly stem from the question of how open one should remain to explanations that are still unknown.

"I understand that people start puzzling over it; I can end up in that situation too," says expert Köhler. "Some people call the police at 2:00 in the morning and say they can see something flashing in the sky. Then the officers call us because the people insist so strongly that there is something there. So you have two police officers standing there, looking up at the sky together with the caller, unable to explain it either and phoning us."

Köhler has a recommendation for such cases: "Members of the public can find out what they are observing – there are free astronomy apps. You can point your phone at the sky and the name of the celestial body then appears."

What has he been able to identify so far?

Aircraft, helicopters, rocket stages, satellites, astronomical causes such as meteors, bright fireballs (daytime meteors), planets, bright stars, balloons of all kinds (weather, atmospheric, hot-air) and decorative foil balloons in XXL format from children's birthday parties and weddings, as well as lasers used by event organisers that sometimes shine over distances of several kilometres.

There are, however, also cases that Köhler has not been able to resolve. Anyone hoping to see them as proof of extraterrestrial visitors will be disappointed: "These were not alien visits. The cases have simply remained unexplained because we lack key information. For a serious investigation we need the date, time, place, direction in the sky and, if possible, visual material. Only then can we start our research."

World.title: Ukraine denies targeting Bulgaria as drone explodes near pipeline, Kyiv promises inquiry
World.content:
Ukraine denied on Saturday targeting Bulgaria after a drone exploded close to the strategic Trans-Balkan gas pipeline linking Turkey to Ukraine near the Romanian border.

 

Bulgaria's defence ministry said the drone was of a type "widely used by the Ukrainian military", and the foreign minister summoned the Ukrainian ambassador for a meeting on Monday in response, her office said.

Kyiv said it was "in close contact with the Bulgarian side to clarify the circumstances" of the incident, the latest case of a drone straying into NATO airspace as Ukraine fights off Russia's invasion.

"We can say with certainty that the Ukrainian Armed Forces did not intentionally direct any assets toward Bulgaria," Ukraine's foreign ministry spokesman Georgiy Tykhyi said, blaming Russia's invasion for the incident.

No casualties reported

While the explosion caused no casualties, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said the amount of explosives it was carrying was "significant".

"The drone exploded in the immediate vicinity of the Kardam border-crossing with Romania," near the Black Sea in the country's northeast, "1,000 metres from the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline's compressor station," he said in a video released by the government.

After analysing the debris from the crash, Bulgaria's defence ministry, however, said that "currently, nothing suggests that this was a deliberate incident".

The drone eventually crashed into a sunflower field, Radev said.

'Significant amount of explosives'

Romania border police recorded the sound of the drone, then a Bulgarian border police patrol spotted "a loud explosion accompanied by black smoke", Radev added, speaking after an extraordinary meeting of his cabinet's security council.

"One thing is certain: the drone was carrying a significant amount of explosives, given that it could be heard from a distance and produced such black smoke," he said.

The drone had not been detected by either of the two neighbouring countries, he said, adding: "As you know, identifying and neutralising these drones poses a major challenge."

Incidents involving drones have become increasingly frequent in recent months across eastern European countries that are NATO members and supporters of Ukraine in its conflict with Russia.

Romania has faced frequent drone incursions since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 — including some crashes on its territory. It ordered the expulsion of a Russian embassy staff member in late July.

Radev said that, following the latest incident, Bulgaria had boosted its surveillance and would redeploy troops and soldiers to the borders to detect drones and employ anti-drone measures.

Turkey asks for 'moratorium'

Bulgaria, Romania, and Turkey all front onto the Black Sea, an arena of drone combat by both Ukraine and Russia which has seen attacks on civilian ships.

Turkey's foreign minister on Saturday called for a "moratorium" on attacks by Russia and Ukraine in the body of water in an interview with Turkey's state news agency Anadolu.

"To begin with, they targeted the ports and the military ships," said Turkish Minister for Foreign Affairs, Hakan Fidan. "Now, they are attacking all commercial shipping without distinction."

Turkey had already on Tuesday denounced Black Sea drone attacks on two Turkish civilian vessels the previous day, in which some crew members were injured.

Bulgaria in June halted its military aid to Ukraine. Radev said the country did not belong in the coalition of Kyiv's allies supplying arms and that he preferred to see diplomatic efforts to end the war.

Further west, a German military operational command spokesman told AFP on Saturday that drones were detected this week above an army installation in western Germany known to house a large underground depot.

Among other armaments, the Mechernich special site is home to parts for US-made Patriot air-defence systems long coveted by Kyiv.

Those sightings came days after an explosives-laden drone was found near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig-Halle airport, which plays a key role in the transport of military goods by the German military and NATO allies.

World.title: Travelling to Qatar? Here’s what you need to know when visiting the Gulf state
World.content:
For many travellers, Qatar may have first come onto their radar in 2022 when it became the first country in the Middle East and North Africa to host the FIFA World Cup – a time I look back on fondly.

 

During the festival of football, the streets of Doha were awash with colour as fans donned national flag-designed “thobes”, which is the men’s traditional attire in the country and region.

Strangers also struck up conversations in every corner of the capital city and there was an atmosphere that felt as though the world truly had descended on this once-overlooked Gulf destination.

However, some of the best gems are beyond the glimmering stadiums. Instead, they are tucked away in the alleyways of the centuries-old Souq Waqif, the serene scenes of the country’s mangrove forest as well as within its desert adventures beyond the capital and arts and culture scenes.

Beyond the Doha skyline, here’s what I wish more travellers knew about the place I call home.

European travellers can visit with minimal hassle

For travellers from the European Union, visiting Qatar is pretty straightforward.

All EU member-state passport holders are eligible for visa-free entry into the country if their passport is valid for at least three months from the date of arrival and if they have a confirmed hotel booking.

Many non-EU European nationals – including travellers from the UK, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Iceland, Azerbaijan and Switzerland – can also benefit from visa-free travel. In total, citizens of more than 102 countries are eligible for visa free entry into the Gulf state.

After landing at Hamad International Airport, visitors can easily explore Doha via a modern metro system.

Souq Waqif is the place to understand traditional Qatar

Nestled in Doha’s old town, Souq Waqif offers a perfect first taste of Qatari culture and heritage with its array of fragrant spice stalls that are overflowing jute sacks of Arabic aromatics such as saffron, zaatar, sumac, dried flowers, dried black lemons and endless varieties of dates, honey, tea leaves and coffee beans.

Here, you can also meet some of the country’s most beloved animals. At the Falcon Souq, shopkeepers are more than happy to have tourists pose with the majestic bird perched on their arm.

Meanwhile, just a stone's throw away, the camel pen homes the doe-eyed creatures. There are also stables that house Arabian horses, that gallop to and from the grounds with heritage equestrians on horseback.

Doha has a serious dining scene

Doha is home to more than 3,000 restaurants, serving up everything from traditional Qatari and Gulf cuisine, to Latin American, Asian and European flavours.

It’s no wonder the city’s culinary scene has attracted the attention of the Michelin Guide, which debuted in the country in 2024. In the Michelin Guide Doha, 41 restaurants are listed, including three that earned a Michelin star and eight with a Bib Gourmand.

For top places to eat in Doha, I recommend the Michelin-listed Kai’s Songbird at Corinthia Yacht Club, and Nota Blu at the Four Seasons The Pearl-Qatar, a Spanish brasserie bringing Mediterranean delights to Doha.

For more casual dining, grab local favourites such as a cup of saffron karak tea and a chapatti from Karak Mqanes.

At Nota Blu Brasserie Doha, try the Sea Bass Puttanesca, the Truffle Mezzi Rigatoni pasta and (if you're not counting the calories) order a creme brulee, too Fakhriya M. Suleiman/Euronews Travel

Sea, desert and wildlife experiences – all in one trip

Because of Qatar’s compact size, travellers can combine dramatically different landscapes in little time.

A visitor in Qatar can quickly move from Doha’s city skyline to having desert and beach adventures without a complicated itinerary.

Desert activities include dune bashing and spotting wildlife such as camels and Arabian oryx, or you can relax at one of the country's array of beaches and beach resorts.

Along the coast, visitors can also explore the country by a traditional dhow boat, paddleboard and kiteboard. Qatar’s surrounding waters are known for marine life, including being home to the world’s second largest population of dugongs.

Home to the region’s famous ‘Inland Sea’

Khor Al Adaid, known as the “Inland Sea”, is one of Qatar’s most striking natural wonders: a landlocked lagoon surrounded by sand dunes of up to 40 metres high.

The water at the Inland Sea is calm and warm, making it safe to swim, with the best time to visit being anywhere from November through to April when the weather is just right.

Other geographical features at this UNESCO-recognised site include rocky ridges and cliffs that are no more than a two-hour drive to the border with Saudi Arabia.

The National Museum of Qatar, Doha Photo by monk 333 on Unsplash

Qatar’s pearl diving history dates back thousands of years

Thousands of years ago, the pearl trade was central to the local economy in Qatar and the first major export commodity. The country is also linked to one of the world’s oldest known natural pearls dating as far back as 4600 BCE.

Today, visitors can take a deep dive into the country’s pearling history at the National Museum of Qatar where prized pearl pieces are on display. Pearls also take centre stage during the annual Doha Jewellery & Watches Exhibition, which will next be held from 28 September to 3 October 2026.

Katara Cultural Village: Art, heritage and performances

Doha’s Katara Cultural Village is well worth a visit. It brings together public art, galleries, performance spaces and impressive architecture showcasing the country’s creativity.

Astronomy enthusiasts and families should check out the Al Thuraya Planetarium which hosts a range of exhibitions on astronomy, atmosphere, geology and the oceans. It also walks visitors through the role of astronomy in Qatar's history and religious traditions.

A stop by Katara’s 21 High Street is unmissable. The luxurious corner of the cultural village features a Galeries Lafayette department store, an outdoor cooling system and is lined with trendy cafes for al fresco dining.

Al fresco dining along Katara’s cooled 21 High Street Fakhriya M. Suleiman/Euronews Travel

A destination for much needed R&R

The Zulal Wellness Resort by Chiva-Som is located north of the country in Al Ruwais. It specialises in traditional Arabic and Islamic medicine, inspired by Ibn Sina’s (Avicenna) Canon of Medicine from 1025. The beachfront sanctuary offers a range of treatments, including physiotherapy, acupuncture, guided meditation as well as pilates and kayaking sessions.

The country’s beach resorts, destination spas, pool clubs and five-star hotels also offer everything from hydrotherapy to fine dining and private beach access.

A family-friendly destination

With a diverse range of things to see and do that are fun for all ages, the Gulf state makes a great option for a family holiday abroad.

There are various theme parks including Angry Birds World, family entertainment venues such as Doha Quest and fun cultural spaces like the Dadu Gardens which offers activities for children aged up to 11-years-old all within close proximity in Doha.

Visit Qatar, the country’s tourism board, also runs its annual “Hala Summer” campaign, which includes a host of freebies to participating attractions and entertainment venues.

Must-see attractions and landmarks in Qatar

Purple Island, near Al Khor

Mina District at Old Doha Port, Doha

Gewan Island, Doha

Msheireb Downtown, Doha

Al Shaqab Equestrian Center, Education City – Doha

Oxygen Park, Education City – Doha

East-West/West-East sculpture by Richard Serra, Brouq Nature Reserve

Al Zubarah Fort, Zubarah

Souq Waqif, Doha

Katara Cultural Village, Doha

World.title: Harvesting rainwater from rooftops could cut the number of heatwave days and reduce air con reliance
World.content:
Rooftop rainwater could be a secret weapon in tackling extreme heat, following Europe’s blistering summer.

 

New research from The University of Manchester in the UK modelled a system that stores rainwater harvested from rooftops and automatically sprays it onto buildings during hot weather.

The study, published in the science journal Earth’s Future, found that cooler roofs transferred less heat into buildings, lowering the demand for air conditioning and therefore cutting energy consumption usually needed for cooling.

Less air con also means less heat waste would be released into the city. Together, researchers say these effects could help reduce urban temperatures, cutting the number of heatwave days overall and lessening the intensity of extreme heat events.

Rooftops can act as ‘strategic cooling’ for cities

The study, which used the city of Tokyo as a case study, suggests that the time at which sprinklers were switched on – for example, when the roof reached a certain temperature – had a greater impact than either the size of the tank or the amount of water applied.

It also found that bigger is not always better. In fact, very large tanks delivered only “modest additional reductions” in energy use and extreme heat, while applying extra water did not always lead to more cooling because some of it remained on the roof instead of evaporating.

“Cities around the world are facing growing challenges from extreme heat,” says lead author Dr Zhonghua Zheng of The University of Manchester.

“Air conditioning can help keep people safe and comfortable but it also consumes large amounts of energy and releases additional heat into the urban environment. Our study shows that harvesting rainwater from roofs and using it strategically for cooling could provide a practical way to reduce both energy demand and urban temperatures.”

Dr Zheng adds that the benefits of harvesting rooftop rainwater become “even greater during hotter years”, suggesting that the approach could become increasingly important as the climate continues to warm.

The study could help local authorities and urban planners evaluate how rainwater-based cooling systems might work in their own regions, while considering practicalities such as cost and water availability.

“The rainwater tank also provides an additional co-benefit on reducing the extreme urban runoff,” says Junjie Yu, PhD researcher at The University of Manchester.

“This approach exemplifies a ‘natural solution to natural challenges’, in which rainwater serves as a natural resource to mitigate both thermal stress and hydrological extremes.”

Why air con isn’t the best way to tackle extreme heat

The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimates that space cooling – which is mostly air conditioning, but also includes fans – consumed around 2,100 terawatt-hours (TWh) of power in 2022. That’s around seven per cent of the world’s electricity from that year.

Experts warn that air con units could triple in the next three decades, reaching a staggering 5.5 billion installations, as extreme heat becomes the ‘new normal’.

It’s triggered concern that increased demand will put additional strain on Europe’s already struggling energy grid, and send emissions spiralling.

While air conditioning could theoretically be powered by clean energy such as solar power, concern remains over the use of refrigerants such as hydrofluorocarbon and hydrochlorofluorocarbon. These are powerful greenhouse gases that trap thousands of times more heat in the atmosphere compared to CO2.

The EU and UK are actively phasing out fluorinated gases in favour of natural refrigerants such as hydrocarbons (like propane) and CO2, which are far less damaging to the climate – but propane’s flammability makes installation complicated.

Still, the very process of absorbing heat from inside a home and dumping it outside contributes to the urban heat island effect. This is when heat is trapped between tall buildings and absorbed by the large amounts of asphalt and concrete found in cities before being released back into the air.

It is why larger cities tend to experience stronger heat stress and higher maximum temperatures than nearby rural areas.

How ‘cool roofs’ can also help tackle heatwaves

A 2024 study by UCL and The University of Exeter analysed the cooling effect that roofs painted white or other reflective colours (known as ‘cool roofs’) would have on London’s air temperature between June and August 2018.

At the time, this was one of the city’s hottest summers on record, with the average temperature during those three months hitting 19.2C – about 1.6C warmer than average for that time of year.

The paper found that had cool roofs been widely installed through London, the city could have cooled by about 0.8C on average.

“If widely adopted, cool roofs can significantly reduce the ground-level air temperature of a city,” says lead author Dr Charles Simpson from the UCL Bartlett School Environment, Energy & Resources.

“The resulting cooling effect across the city would save lives and improve the quality of life for residents throughout the urban area.”

World.title: Turkey's new opposition party offers hope, but its future is already in jeopardy
World.content:
The launch of the Yeni Party in Turkey promises to energise the country's struggling opposition. But while some polls show it leading, it remains vulnerable – already beset by arrests it says are "politically motivated".

Advertising

In a glitzy video, set to pumping music and shared widely across social media, Ozgur Ozel launched the Yeni Party – "New Party" – vowing to usher in a new era in Turkish politics and end President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s long rule.

Ozel founded the New Party after a court removed him from leading the main opposition party, the Republican People’s Party (CHP).

His rival, former party leader Kemal Kilicdaroglu, 77, who lost every election during his decade in charge of the CHP, replaced him.

Many in the country believe Erdogan played a role in the removal of Ozel, as his popularity grew thanks to tireless campaigning.

Riding the wave

The New Party is settings its sights beyond the CHP’s usual supporters.

"It covers the whole political spectrum in Turkish political life," explains Ozel's advisor Ilham Uzel.

"There are critical elements like democratisation, rule of law, secularism and a pro-Western approach, so we maintain these main pillars. But it is not confined to social democracy; we reach out to every section of Turkish society, including Islamists and conservatives, nationalists and liberals. We have Kurdish supporters."

The New Party is riding a wave of excitement. Ninety-one out of 135 CHP parliamentary deputies have defected to its ranks, joined by dozens of mayors and it is swiftly becoming the main opposition in parliament.

Turkey opposition worries that Europe is sacrificing democracy for security

Some polls show the party soaring above 30 percent, leaving Erdogan’s Justice and Development Party behind, while the CHP’s support has collapsed.

The New Party’s broad approach is finding fertile ground. "Even those who still support the governing coalition, the AK Party and MHP, are unhappy with how things are or how politics is practised, especially regarding economic issues. So there is a push towards change," says political commentator Sezin Oney.

"There is a yearning to change things at the grassroots, and the New Party may be the only party that can represent a new way of doing politics. But they have to live up to it, of course."

Corruption charges

Erdogan has remained in power for more than 20 years partly by exploiting divisions within the opposition, which is made up of conservatives, hardline secularists, and both Kurdish and Turkish nationalists.

The New Party has a key advantage over the strongly secular CHP, whose history is linked to past policies targeting Turkey’s large Kurdish minority and religious conservatives.

"CHP is identified with many bad experiences that the Kurds and conservative people had in past decades," said Mesut Yegen of the Diyarbakir-based Kurdish Studies Center.

"If you look at what Ozgur Ozel says during his speeches, you may clearly see the Yeni Party doesn’t have the baggage of CHP."

Erdogan has also often exploited the CHP’s history, painting it as anti-religious and hostile to Kurdish minority rights. The New Party faces the tricky task of keeping CHP loyalists on board while reaching new supporters.

But for now, simply staying out of jail may be the most pressing concern for its representatives.

Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended

Several mayors who joined the New Party have been arrested on corruption charges, widely seen as politically motivated. In the past two years, 26 opposition mayors and hundreds of officials have been imprisoned on corruption allegations, compared to two mayors from Erdogan’s AK Party.

"They are cracking down on our party – every other day, mayors are arrested," says Uzgel. "They filed another charge against our leader. Nobody is safe in this authoritarian regime. So Mr Ozel is on the spot, definitely."

Ozel is protected by parliamentary immunity, but Oney warns he may be running out of time.

"Ozgur Ozel might be imprisoned himself once his immunity is removed by a parliamentary vote, that's a possibility. The only immunity he can have is the immunity bestowed upon him by the people. So only public opinion is protecting him. How much can it protect him? We'll see."

With parliament about to break for summer until October, Ozel has a brief window to strengthen his party and rally public support.

World.title: Study: Obesity 'bigger cancer risk' than previously thought
World.content:
A new study has found that being significantly overweight could be responsible for more cases of cancer than previously known. Abdominal fat, in particular, increases the risk of cancer — especially among women.

Being overweight or obese significantly increases the risk of developing colon cancer, breast cancer or liver cancer, and is a major risk factor for 10 other types of cancer, a new study has found.

Until recently, researchers believed that 2% to 8% of all cancer cases were attributable to excess body weight. But a new study by a team led by Hermann Brenner, an epidemiologist with the German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ), suggests that this was a serious underestimate.

According to the study, up to 11.5% of cancers may be attributable to being overweight.

The DKFZ researchers "have not only updated existing risk estimates, but have also questioned whether the link between excess weight and cancer may have been underestimated until now," Michael Leitzmann, an epidemiologist at the University of Regensburg, told DW.

Leitzmann, who was not involved in the study, researches diet, body weight, physical activity and the development of chronic diseases at the university's Institute of Epidemiology and Prevention, and has advised German Cancer Aid.

The abdominal-fat 'trigger'

The DKFZ team changed its research methods for the new study. Previous research used body mass index (BMI), which is calculated based on height and weight, as an indicator of excess weight. But BMI does not distinguish between fat and muscle mass, and does not provide information on how fat is distributed throughout the body.

This is important, because not all fat is the same. Fat cells that accumulate around the abdomen are more than just a passive store for excess calories, unlike those in other parts of the body. "They trigger what is known as a chronic inflammatory metabolic state," Leitzmann said.

Excess abdominal fat functions like a gland that releases various signaling molecules, known as adipokines. These travel through the bloodstream to different parts of the body, where they influence other metabolic processes — including cell growth and division, as well as the inhibition of programmed cell death. "These are all mechanisms that can contribute to the development and subsequent growth of tumors," Leitzmann said.

The DKFZ researchers therefore focused not only on BMI but also on waist circumference and the waist-to-hip ratio. Data from 458,543 women and men from the UK Biobank , which holds one of the world's biggest health datasets, were included in the study. The participants were followed for and average of 12 years, during which 50,000 new cases of cancer were identified.

Understanding previous underestimates

The researchers wanted to rule out a potential methodological bias in previous studies: the fact that cancer can lead to weight loss even before diagnosis — that is, while it is still developing.

That suggests that previous studies failed to identify a link between obesity and cancer because the participants had already lost weight because they had developed cancer by the time they entered the study.

For this reason, the team excluded the first few years following the participants' enrollment from the analysis. Only cancer cases that occurred seven years after the start of the observation period were considered — and that made the statistical link between being overweight and cancer clearer.

How AI is expanding breast cancer screening in Mexico To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Women at risk

The study suggests that the proportion of overweight women who develop cancer is higher than that of men, but Leitzmann urges caution when interpreting these findings. Further studies with a similar design are needed to see whether the results can be replicated.

Leitzmann offered a theory on why being overweight might have a more severe impact on women. Being overweight is blamed, among other things, for breast, uterine and ovarian cancers. "These types of cancer, which affect women, are hormone-dependent," Leitzmann said. For example, the hormone estrogen can stimulate the growth of breast cancer, and excess abdominal fat can contribute to elevated estrogen levels.

Most people are now aware that obesity increases the risk of cardiovascular disease or Type 2 diabetes, Leitzmann said. Conversely, this also means that people who lose weight also reduce their risk of heart attacks, strokes and diabetes.

Though the DKFZ study emphasizes the increased risk associated with obesity, Leitzmann said the findings were also a reason for optimism: "To me, this clearly indicates that, by preventing obesity, we will be able to make a greater contribution to cancer prevention than previously assumed."

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Indonesia: Mount Bromo wildfire grows, spurs park closure
World.content:
Indonesian authorities have closed a popular national park until further notice. Strong winds and rough terrain are making it difficult for firefighters to extinguish the blaze.

Authorities in Indonesia closed the Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park in East Java until further notice on Saturday due to a wildfire that has scorched some 176 hectares (435 acres) of land on Mount Bromo since it began on Monday.

The blaze, one of several currently burning across Indonesia, has mobilized hundreds of firefighters, park rangers, police, soldiers and volunteers at one of Indonesia's most popular tourist destinations.

What do we know about the wildfires situation in Indonesia?

Helicopters and drones are in use in the air and firebreaks are being created by crews on the ground.

Officials describe the situation as challenging, pointing to high winds and rough terrain, with many areas difficult to access on steep volcanic slopes.

"These conditions make air operations important to reach areas that cannot be accessed optimally by land," one official said.

The blaze has mobilized hundreds of firefighters, park rangers, police, soldiers and volunteers at one of Indonesia's most popular tourist destinations Image: Muhammad Fajri/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

Dry conditions and winds are fueling the spread of the flames according to Indonesia's Meteorological, Climatological and Geophysical Agency.

Authorities say the fire was sparked during land clearing work.

Though fires — often illegally started by plantation owners and farmers to clear for planting — are common in the region, the current El Nino weather pattern and seasonal dry winds from Australia have combined to make this year especially prone to wildfire and drought.

Indonesia has lost more than 107,000 hectares of land to fire in the first half of 2026, over twice the area destroyed in wildfires in 2023, when the last El-Nino pattern started.

08/09/2026 August 9, 2026 Instant payments will remain free for users, government clarifies

The Indian government has clarified that its real-time payment service, called Unified Payments Interface (UPI), will remain free-of-charge for consumers. It said only merchants will have to pay a "nominal" charge for some transactions.

The clarification came after the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 was passed in Lok Sabha earlier this week. The bill caused much concern over a potential charge on UPI transactions.

Earlier reports had suggested that the bill would allow the government to permit banks and payment companies to charge fees on UPI and other digital payments in the future.

Addressing the concern, the Ministry of Finance clarified that all person-to-person transactions will remain free of charge.

It however said that a limited set of merchant transactions will incur transaction charges when the MDR (Merchant Discount Rate) charges are introduced.

MDR is a fee levied on merchants by banks to help meet costs related to processing of transactions, settlement and infrastructure.

Since its introduction by the Reserve Bank of India in 2016, UPI has become one of the most popular payment methods across the country.

In 2025 alone, the UPI transaction load stood at 228.5 billion transactions in India. The total value of UPI transactions reached Rs 299.74 trillion (€2.7 trillion, $3.4 trillion).

World.title: Australia: Jetstar, Qatar Airways planes almost collide on Sydney Airport tarmac
World.content:
A flight crew member was injured in a near-miss collision on the runway at Australia's Sydney Airport. An investigation has been launched to determine what caused the incident.

Two passenger aircraft — a Jetstar and a Qatar Airways plane — came close to crashing into each other on the tarmac at Australia's busiest Sydney Airport on Sunday.

A crew member was injured and the incident has triggered a probe by the country's safety regulators.

What do we know about the near-miss collision?

The Jetstar A320 was taxiing for takeoff to the Gold Coast in the state of Queensland when its flight crew saw the Qatar Airways Boeing 777 — which was being towed by an aircraft tug — in close proximity on a crossing taxiway, the Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) said in a statement.

"Both aircraft were stopped abruptly", the statement said, leading to a Jestar cabin crew member moving through the cabin being injured and the connection between the 777 nose gear and aircraft tug suffering damage.

The injured crew member was treated by paramedics.

How are Australian authorities handling the incident?

The ATSB said that investigators were gathering data from both the planes, air traffic control, and interviewing crew and tug operators to determine the cause of the near collision.

The regulator put out a call for witnesses at the airport to send in any visuals of the incident.

Jetstar — which is a low-cost subsidiary of Australia's national carrier Qantas — said it was also conducting its own investigation.

"Our aircraft was following ⁠instructions ​by Air Traffic Control when the ​pilots were forced to brake firmly after another aircraft came in ​close proximity," a ‌Jetstar spokesperson said.

There was no immediate statement from Qatar Airways, which is the flag carrier of Qatar.

Meanwhile, flights at Sydney Airport were experiencing delays following the incident, government agency Airservices Australia said.

Sunday's incident ⁠comes a day after Sydney Airport witnessed widespread delays ⁠sparked by Airservices Australia authorizing "departure spacing" due to roster issues with air traffic controllers.

08/09/2026 August 9, 2026 Germany's trade deficit with China grows in first half

New preliminary data released on Sunday has shown that German exports to China fell more than 12% year-on-year between January to June, while German imports from China rose 8.9%.

That raises last year's trade deficit of €40 billion ($46.2 billion) for the same period to some €55 billion.

The data from the state-run agency Germany Trade & Invest (GTAI) reflects the decreasing reliance by Chinese firms on European imports.

They show that although China remains Germany's top trading partner, the Asian powerhouse is now only the ninth-biggest market for German goods, with far smaller economies like Austria and Switzerland buying more from Germany in 2026.

As recently as 2021, China was Germany's second-biggest ​export market.

The US remains Germany's single-biggest foreign market, despite a drop in German exports there amid protectionist tariffs introduced under President Donald Trump.

World.title: Canada: British Columbia declares emergency as fires spread
World.content:
More than 20,000 people have been forced from their homes by out-of-control wildfires in Canada's British Columbia, where 105 blazes are currently burning.

Canadian officials on Saturday declared a state of emergency in British Columbia after more than 20,000 people were ordered to flee a fast-moving wildfire.

Describing the intensity of the blaze, British Columbia Premier David Eby said a fire official compared it to "a bomb going off."

"He described flames on a 100-foot (30-meter) tree, flames going 200 feet above that, and the fire creating its own weather system, which creates lightning," Eby said.

"Homes have been lost, and properties have been destroyed. Some people became trapped as conditions changed very quickly, and needed to be rescued," he added.

Wildfire in British Columbia nearly doubles in size overnight

The fire, first reported Friday evening, grew rapidly overnight, triggering widespread evacuation orders.

By Saturday, it had spread to about 9,500 hectares (23,500 acres), prompting all 12,000 residents of the Summerland district to evacuate.

The Summerland blaze is one of many fires challenging emergency crews across British Columbia.

The province has seen 70 new wildfires over the past week, and 105 are currently burning, according to British Columbia Minister of Forests Ravi Parmar.

A dry and hot summer has ⁠led to more than ​4,500 fires in Canada this year [FILE: August 3, 2026] Image: Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/picture alliance

Canada grapples with large wildfires

Fires have scorched 4 million hectares in Canada in 2026, according to the Canadian Interagency Forest Fire Center .

Blazes flared up in several regions, including Ontario and Quebec, this year as hot, dry conditions fueled fires in dense forest areas.

In recent years, Canada has faced a growing number of destructive wildfire seasons.

World.title: FIFA warns against 'concerted effort' to undermine Gianni Infantino
World.content:
Pressure is mounting on the FIFA president Gianni Infantino after plans to sell a stake in the World Cup collapsed and fresh allegations emerged relating to his time at UEFA.

FIFA warned against what it calls a "concerted and ongoing effort" to "undermine" the organization and its president, Gianni Infantino.

The statement, issued late on Saturday, comes amid a growing dispute over Infantino's leadership after the failed plan to create a subsidiary to run the men's World Cup and other events, with up to a 20% stake offered to external investors.

The proposal drew criticism from European governing body UEFA, which threatened to boycott future World Cups, as well as several national associations and senior FIFA officials, and prompted calls for Infantino to resign.

Amid the growing criticism Infantino persuaded FIFA's Board of Management to express its full support for him at a crisis meeting in Rabat, Morocco, on Wednesday.

FIFA accused of blackmail in exchange for Infantino support To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Report raises new questions over Infantino

The pressure on Infantino intensified on Friday when British newspaper the Daily Telegraph reported a six-figure sum was paid to a female employee alleged to have been in a relationship with him during his time as UEFA general secretary.

UEFA confirmed a departure payment and said it also funded her MBA course, stating both were in line with regulations at the time.

A FIFA spokesman told the Telegraph on Friday: "FIFA president Gianni Infantino strongly denies these allegations, and they are categorically untrue."

Responding to the latest scrutiny, FIFA said on Saturday, without directly mentioning the Telegraph report, "recent reporting has included unsubstantiated assertions and demonstrably false claims concerning FIFA and its President."

Investment plan dispute deepens leadership crisis

The fallout over the shelved private investment plan has overshadowed Infantino's bid for a fourth term as FIFA president.

After this week's crisis meeting, UEFA said it no longer has confidence in him, and Norwegian FA President Lise Klaveness called for his resignation.

Despite the controversy, Infantino retains strong backing among FIFA members, with the Confederation of African Football (CAF) unanimously supporting his leadership and South American governing body CONMEBOL opposing any attempt to remove him without a vote of all member associations.

FIFA said that those who lacked the support of its member associations should not seek to achieve "allegation, insinuation or misinformation what they cannot achieve through FIFA's established democratic processes."

World.title: Germany: Interior Minister warns of 'daily' hybrid warfare
World.content:
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt says attacks by foreign powers have become a constant threat to Germany. His remarks come just days after an explosive-laden drone was found at Leipzig airport.

Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt on Sunday warned that hybrid warfare attacks had become a daily threat to the country.

"We're not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare," Dobrindt told the newspaper Bild am Sonntag following the discovery of a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig/Halle Airport.

"Espionage, sabotage, cyberattacks, or covert operations by foreign powers aimed at destabilizing Germany or inflicting direct harm are a constant reality," Dobrindt said.

He also noted that the country is stepping up research into drones to address new security threats.

A new drone security research center will be established later in August at a German Aerospace Center (DLR) test airport in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, Dobrindt said.

Drone warfare: German startup draws on Ukraine's experience To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Drones spotted above military base in west Germany

On Saturday, Germany's armed forces confirmed that two drones had been spotted late on Thursday over a German military base in Mechernich in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia near the Belgian border.

The drones were detected at around 10 p.m. (2000 GMT) over the Bundeswehr base, a German armed forces spokesperson said.

German media reported that the base hosts personnel responsible for the maintenance of US Patriot air defense systems, which play a key role in defending Ukraine against Russian aerial attacks.

Drone incident at Leipzig airport

The sighting in Mechernich comes just two days after the discovery of a drone carrying explosives a Ukrainian transport plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport, an incident Dobrindt called a "hybrid attack scenario."

While German government officials have refrained from publicly blaming any foreign country over the Leipzig incident, some lawmakers have pointed fingers at Russia, which has been at war with Ukraine since ​its full-scale invasion of the country in 2022.

On Friday, the Russian Embassy in Berlin dismissed the Leipzig event as a "fabricated provocation" and said Russia was once more being accused of hostile actions "without the slightest evidence being presented."
