World.title: Climate: things are going to get ugly
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Climate: things are going to get ugly August 9, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Badiucao To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. CLIMATE SOLUTIONS Thank you for your recent articles about climate change and the need to adapt to it (“Ready or Not”, Good Weekend, 8/8, and ″⁣Fire, flood and wishful thinking: Why we’re not ready for Victoria’s climate future″⁣, 9/8).

I have never really wanted to ″⁣accept″⁣ adaptation because it clearly means we have not reduced emissions satisfactorily, despite decades of warning.

Sadly, Australia has not done nearly enough about reducing emissions (think of Scope 3 – the emissions we export), nor nearly enough planning or enacting adaptation schemes.

This is simply poor governance. We have been led by political parties that either do as little as they can plausibly get away with, or by being downright climate change deniers.

We will pay an extremely heavy price for this inactivity that I do not believe we truly understand. This could, or will, get ugly.

Phil Labrum, Trentham We’d rather chuck another prawn on the barbie

Your Climate solutions series including “Fire, flood and wistful thinking” (9/8) is already a damning indictment of Victoria’s political leadership over decades – and, because climate impacts don’t stop at the Murray, of Australia’s, too.

From Mooroopna’s 2022 flood to underfunding of identified resilience strategies; from this year’s report warning of more than $300 billion coastal damage this century to the cost-saving

abolition of the advisory council which made it; from West Kinglake’s 2009 devastation to a rebuilt enclave – with the state “spending vastly less on preparing for the future than on responding to natural disasters”.

But tales of past “violent weather, sea-level rise, flood, fire and drought” – and woeful preparation for more – no longer shock.

Nor do they just condemn our leaders. We, the voting citizenry, have been effectively seduced by both blatant and insidious siren songs of endless consumer prosperity to the extent that it is now regarded as a right.

Thus, we have resisted and rejected options to build safer communities, the equitable (and considerable) taxation it requires, and any politician or party foolish enough to propose them.

Measured across the nation, our democratic priorities have been bigger houses, flasher and more powerful cars etc – and increased inequality and the freedoms to go with them. We’d rather chuck another prawn on the barbie.

So we bid fair to become metaphorical prawns ourselves.

Ken Blackman, Inverloch



Australia, world leader in gas expansion

Unfortunately for all residents of the planet, our governments seem quite able to ignore the “enormous and unconscionable impact” of our coal and gas exports (Letters, 9/8).

How else can we explain the fact that for the years between the 2015 Paris Agreement and 2024, Australia, the world’s 55th most populous nation, ranked fifth in the list of 15 countries responsible for nearly 80 per cent of global oil and gas extraction? We actually led all 15 for rate of gas and oil production increase – up 77 per cent, including a doubling of gas production.

We’re in a climate crisis and a cost-of-living crisis.

But Australia is leading the world in its rate of gas expansion, and still not getting paid for a lot of it. Talk about please explain.

Lesley Walker, Northcote Earth, a people-less future

Your correspondent (Letters, 8/8) states that Earth has existed for billions of years and the climate continually changes. That is correct, except this time it will in all probability survive for billions of years without humans.

We will disappear and become extinct like the other 99.9 per cent of all species that have lived on our fragile planet.

Greg Lawes, Dingley Village THE FORUM Melbourne survival plan

Oh, how things have changed. In the 1990s, I would think nothing of spending time in the City of Melbourne without fear or worry of danger. I would wander the city looking for restaurants and cafes to relax and spend time and just sit watching the night life, and catching up with friends.

This coming weekend, I am reluctantly travelling into Melbourne to see a theatre show and will stay overnight in a hotel.

My new survival plan is to see the show on Saturday at 2pm and head back to my hotel room (collecting takeaway on the way back to eat in my room) and not leave my room until the next morning when I will catch the train and return home.

So much lost opportunity to explore and revisit the city I used to love.

Yes, I have lost my nerve when I visit Melbourne and some other urban areas.

Alan Parker Jones, Sunbury Uni cancel culture

What a shame that academics cannot tolerate scholarships at Melbourne University from the Ramsay Centre, (“Scholarships worth $35m go begging at university”, 9/8) because its perspectives and philosophy clashes with their preferred world views. This is a lost opportunity for spirited discussion and debate.

Contrasting ideas could be explored rather than being crushed. Students could be taught both how to agree and disagree in thoughtful ways.

However, it seems that cancel culture has its claw-like grip on academia.

Perhaps these academics think they have no choice, or they will be demeaned and cancelled by their rigid colleagues. This has an unfortunate resonance with totalitarian societies.

Pia Brous, Armadale



Trigger warning

When universities continue to complain about their financial straits, how short-sighted and hypocritical not to accept the good faith largesse of the Ramsay Centre for Western Civilisation scholarships for students.

Universities should not be run along ideological paradigms.

They are meant to be bastions of higher learning and that might mean – trigger warning – learning about events, philosophies and ideas that are contested or conservative.

True scholarship is about unearthing facts you may not like even, or especially, if they are irrefutable.

This is the point of intellectual discourse.

The University of Melbourne – my university – should not be afraid to award scholarships that advance knowledge, understanding and the nuanced study of context in different times and places.

University should be the place where minds remain open to differing worldviews, not closed by the pettiness of ideological intransigence.

Ann Rennie, Surrey Hills Hanson’s Uber cut

Pauline Hanson, in her drive to cut migration, wants to target Uber drivers among other classes of employees. As a person who doesn’t have access to taxpayer-funded Commonwealth cars and who hasn’t been gifted an aeroplane, I find Ubers not only extremely useful but I also often find chatting with the drivers an interesting and rewarding experience.

Jan Downing, Hawthorn East Liberals never young

Under Ben Carroll, Victorian Labor has renewed policy and management to benefit it at the November election (“Carroll faces battle for seat as Libs’ treaty pledge falls flat″⁣, 9/8).

Against One Nation, the Liberals need a similar policy upgrade both at the state level and nationally.

The Liberals have sidelined young people in particular, by the outright rejection of climate change nationally plus Treaty and conservation in Victoria. Treaty is in place, climate change will be determined by scientific research not politics, and conservation enjoys high support. So, it’s time to be more adventurous.

Malcolm Cameron, Camberwell Sewerage and the city

There is much talk about the debt that Victoria has incurred to fund the infrastructure Big Build to secure the future of Melbourne.

It has reminded me that when the Labor lord mayor of Brisbane, Clem Jones, was elected in 1961, most of Brisbane was still unsewered.

The city was served by backyard dunnies and a large workforce of dunny men. Jones immediately set about to sewer the city and went into debt to do so.

At the time, the conservative opposition cried foul and argued that he was creating a debt burden for future generations. Jones ignored them and got on with sewering the city, arguing that future generations should help pay for the work as they would be the ones who would most benefit.

By the end of the 1960s, most of the city was sewered. With Brisbane now hosting the Olympic Games, I have visions that but for the leadership of Clem Jones, the venues would have rows and rows of little dunny houses with dunny men running in and out all day.

Ronald Harper, Camberwell Insiders job

Congratulations to the ABC’s Insiders program which celebrated its 25th birthday yesterday.

This celebratory program was a wonderful look back on the past

25 years of politics in Australia.

The quality of the journalism, analytical thinking and the coming together of different political views on this show’s panel over the past 25 years shows us how rational discussion can take place.

We don’t have to agree with each other but we do need to listen and accept that there are a variety of views in politics.

Marilyn Hoban, Mornington



Ups and downs

Some Age journalists appear to have embraced the “uptick”. I must be a grammatical Luddite, but is an uptick the same as an increase? If so, then why not use increase, which I think many readers of my age would understand?

After all, an increase has an opposite – decrease. Does an uptick have an opposite, like a downtick?

Then how does one draw a downtick? To my understanding, ticks always went up!

Then, they were just – wait for it – ticks. And the opposite was a cross.

And don’t get me started on the use of “going forward”. Doesn’t that just mean, in the future?

Could someone please help me understand why it is necessary to complicate simple, understandable English terms?

Eugene Docherty, Bentleigh East Defence overspend

It is scandalous that the United States, China and Russia spend so much money on offensive and defensive weapons.

The US is developing its

$262 billion Golden Dome defence shield (″⁣Space-based missile shield″⁣, 9/8) at the same time as it jointly expends vast sums with Australia on AUKUS nuclear submarines.

The US is also spending

$560 million to develop a mine in Australia to produce scandium, a rare mineral which is vital to its defence industry (″⁣Pentagon in $560 million Aussie mine deal″⁣, 9/8). What a shame these sums of money could not be used for peaceful endeavours.

John Guy, Elsternwick Thanking medicos

Ruby Atkinson’s moving article (″⁣I’m alive today thanks to strangers who don’t even know my name″⁣, 9/8) about her leukaemia diagnosis and treatment is a timely reminder that modern medicine is never the work of one remarkable individual. Behind every outcome stands a team of people — doctors, nurses, pathology and radiology technicians, pharmacists, cleaners, technicians, ward clerks, and countless others, most of whom patients may never see or know by name, as Ruby notes.

When we are at our most vulnerable, these strangers bring not only knowledge and skill, but kindness, reassurance, and hope. They work long and taxing hours, often without public recognition, united by a common purpose: to help another person.

Ruby’s gratitude reminds us that healthcare is built on teamwork, compassion, and quiet dedication.

To every member of those healthcare teams: thank you.

Bryan Walpole, retired emergency physician, Sandy Bay, Tas Football brain health

There has been an outpouring of opinion – mostly highly critical – about Geelong Football Club’s handling of their player in regards to his future brain health. But I have yet to hear any significant discussion about what they actually should do in such cases.

Should they make him wear a helmet, or coach him to protect his head even if it means avoiding a contest for the ball, or expose him to risk and pay him compensation later? Or, should they simply not select him to play?

It’s easy to criticise the action someone else has chosen; far

more challenging to recommend an alternative.

David Francis, Ivanhoe East Perfect day

The drive from the Yarra Valley into the MCG took us just over an hour. My disabled parking permit afforded us four hours in a two-hour bay with a short walk to the ground.

The complimentary mobility shuttle took us to the gate. And, thanks to the generosity of a family member, our tickets to the game were gifted to us.

The predicted rain didn’t fall, and instead we were treated to blue skies. We had a close-up view of Harvey Langford’s possible mark of the year.

And to top it off, the Melbourne Demons beat top of the ladder Fremantle Dockers by four points.

A perfect Saturday afternoon in Melbourne. And just for the record, no Range Rover, no cheese board at half-time and no annual trips to the snow!

Sophie Sadowska, Don Valley



AND ANOTHER THING Treaty

That Jess Wilson still wants to remove the treaty with Victoria’s Indigenous people shows she is out of touch and unelectable.

Paul Thomas, Essendon Jess Wilson’s stated aim to repeal Victoria’s Indigenous treaty legislation within her first 100 days in office just demonstrates how unsuitable the Liberals are for office.

Reg Murray, Glen Iris I listened to the Welcome to the Country message (9/8) before the South Sydney v Parramatta NRL game and thought how simple and beautiful it was. I found it more meaningful than the other introductions to most high-profile sporting games.

Rick Whitelaw, Anglesea



Furthermore

Is it just me who has absolutely no interest in ever having a humanoid robot? I’m fine with something that folds my washing and does the dishes (and all manner of other household chores), but why on earth does it need to look like a human?

Sam Branigan, St Kilda Did the Australian Catholic Bishops Conference discuss how expensive religious schools are contributing to growing social division? No, I thought not.

Paula O’Brien, St Kilda Long may television programs such as the ABC’s Insiders exist – 25 years of discussion from various viewpoints, political foibles skewered, a show worth more than its parts. Political parties that wish to curtail funding for the ABC should be put on notice.

Peter Roche, Carlton AFL

Considering Geelong Football Club’s position on concussion, it would be appropriate if

Kardinia Park’s name was changed to Dangerfield.

Garry Adams, Corio As an Essendon Bombers tragic, I have now asked for the intercession of the patron saint of “impossible causes” to come on board. Nothing on the human

level seems to hold weight. Welcome aboard, St Jude!

Tris Raouf, Hadfield The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Geelong deserve a hefty fine, but the fallout of the Kolodjashnij case will be much more significant
World.content:
Four Points SportAFLAFL 2026 Geelong deserve a hefty fine, but the fallout of the Kolodjashnij case will be much more significant Peter Ryan August 9, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading Key points Geelong are likely to cop a heavy financial hit over Jake Kolodjashnij - which they should.

The ‘King of Melbourne’ and the game of the year on Saturday.

Only one man mattered to Collingwood on Sunday.

Matt Rowell has returned to his best.

The two areas in which Geelong failed in the process which enabled premiership defender Jake Kolodjashnij to continue his career in 2024 after the independent concussion panel’s findings added rather than reduced complexity to decisions about his footballing future are clear enough by now. The document which Kolodjashnij, his family and his experienced insurance advisor Adriana Oreskov agreed to with the club should have been lodged by Geelong with the AFL and the players’ association. Jake Kolodjashnij unwittingly found himself at the centre of a football furore. AFL Photos via Getty Images Although it may not have been at the time, it is clear to everyone now, including people within the AFL who were a sounding board for discussions happening between the Cats and Kolodjashnij’s team about a way forward, that the agreement was an extension to the standard playing contract (Kolodjashnij’s deal still had a year to run when the extra agreement was reached).



There is also acknowledgement the document went too far in including a significant line, which AFL chairman then Cats’ president Craig Drummond described in his statement as “a waiver” or, on more generous interpretations, an acknowledgment of risk. It was unnecessary and probably not worth the paper it was written on given you can’t waive occupational health and safety rights. Loading For those two reasons, the Cats are likely to cop a heavy financial penalty, which they should. The rules set out through the collective bargaining agreement exist for a reason and penalties for transgressions, whether deliberate or not, should be applied consistently across the board. Just ask Carlton.



And Geelong should recognise that despite their efforts in recent seasons the exceptionalism that took hold for a period of time post-2022 has no one in any mood to give them the benefit of the doubt in this case. The AFL’s roadblocks and attempts to be clever whenever the media search for answers on issues have also created suspicion and doubt whenever their leaders speak. View post on X But the other questions surrounding this issue, the player’s and the club’s motivation for wanting and then reaching an agreement are not as cut and dried. The implications of concussion has put clubs, players and doctors into a medico-legal-insurance reality that is so complex it is understood by very few players or managers let alone supporters.



The reality raises moral and ethical questions that have not yet been as fully aired as they need to be when clubs are confronted with the considerations Kolodjashnij and Geelong had to contemplate in late 2023, early 2024. Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 The Cats are not the cultural beacon they once claimed to be Caroline Wilson Football columnist for The Age The harsh reality is that doctors and insurers are well down the track of walking away from the game because of the risks player injury exposes them to. Personal insurance has dried up for players, premiums are rising for doctors and clubs and who is liable is an issue. Clubs and players want the game and careers to thrive but they are justifiably worried about where head injuries are taking the game and what has happened to people post-career. That is what officials mean when they use the word complex which AFLPA CEO James Gallagher emphasised on SEN on Friday night.



“There is a concussion challenge in the game and the players are at risk and the game needs to have a safety network for them and we need to ensure we keep the best medical people in the game as well. They probably at this point unfortunately feel a bit of exposure as well,” Gallagher said. Which brings us back to the Kolodjashnij case. The premiership defender wanted to continue his career post the panel finding but it was not as simple as the Cats saying yes or no. Informed consent was needed from Kolodjashnij to a level which satisfied the club doctors, insurers of both clubs and doctors, the club and his family (his brother Kade had retired due to concussion) who all had a stake in his decision. Over a two-month process, the club and Kolodjashnij’s representatives developed a document which satisfied all those stakeholders that informed consent was understood and given, an agreement based on previous documents created for sportspeople in similar situations.



Oreskov was his representative. Her company OSE Advisory has his brother and other retired players Marcus Adams and Paddy McCartin offering testimonials on their website as to her work in assisting them navigating insurance policies and claims. In this case Kolodjashnij found a way towards continuing his career with a representative who had expertise in how to mitigate risk while giving informed consent. He has played 35 AFL games over the past three seasons (he missed 2025 because of other injuries). Without revealing the significance of his discussions, he told me at the end of 2024 he had carefully considered his decision to play on. “There were definitely some tough conversations in pre-season but I am thankful that I chose to keep going and push through and it has paid off,” Kolodjashnij said. Kolodjashnij and his club won’t feel it now but this controversy must force the sensitive discussions happening within clubs and between players into the open so the game confronts what is required to support the players, the doctors, the club boards and the legal experts who are operating on the concussion frontline.



The King of Melbourne inspires the game of the year On Saturday Melbourne played in the manner Steven King imagined when he integrated high speed running into their pre-season and promised the team would play fast football. They have now played in three of the best matches of the season with the Dockers’ clash in front of their wins over the Brisbane Lions and Collingwood at the MCG. Bailey Laurie celebrates the Demons’ win with coach Steven King. AFL Photos The ball flew from end to end as the Demons took their score past 100 points for the fourth time in six matches, having stopped in the nervous nineties in the other two matches.



But the biggest roar from the excited members came at the end of a frenetic passage of play in the middle of the ground after a centre bounce during the second quarter when Melbourne would not let the Dockers execute a clean possession, the ferocity of their tackling a wake-up call to the competition. It was finals football in the middle of the MCG with 40,938 people making the same sound as 80,000 normally do at the home of footy. The highlights from both teams were plentiful with Harry Sharp’s late soccer goal and Patrick Voss’s running goal just before half-time were memorable as the game swung on centre bounce clearances, with eight goals coming from that source. In just his second season Harvey Langford showed why the Demons were so keen to add him to their list with pick six in the 2024 national draft. Max Gawn had a fierce battle against Fremantle’s Luke Jackson at the MCG. Getty Images



He was not their best player but his efforts on the wing in front of the member’s stand symbolised the club’s resurgence under King. His mark of the year contender in the third quarter was exhilarating but the tackle he laid on Matt Johnson and the strong one-on-one mark he took over when the game was on the line in the final quarter was equally meritorious. Melbourne’s members are now treating first year coach Steven King with the same reverence Collingwood supporters treated Craig McRae in 2022. They even stood and applauded him as he worked the boundary in the Saturday afternoon shadows following their victory. Like the Magpies of 2022, the Demons don’t give up. Their ability to hit back whenever they fall behind on the scoreboard was again apparent against the Dockers, who will be a tougher proposition with Alex Pearce playing in defence. King has the team believing. Winning the flag is no longer unrealistic.



Young Collingwood Injured Magpie Scott Pendlebury streamed vision on YouTube of himself alone at home on the couch watching Collingwood qualify for the wildcard round against the Eagles. The 38-year-old’s groaning and involuntary twitching showed the result meant as much to him to Pies’ fans who faced the game with trepidation. The champion was one of the five changes which saw Jordan De Goey, Jeremy Howe, Patrick Lipinski and Harry Perryman take 1258 games out of the team to be replaced by five players with 60 games of experience combined. Nick Daicos is rewriting the record books AFL Photos via Getty Images But only one man mattered to the Magpies chances and he wore No.35.



Nick Daicos was again sublime as he cemented himself as the best player in the game, with a little over a month to wait before he surely wins his first Brownlow Medal. Dan McStay, who is going through his best patch of form during his time at Collingwood, was important at one end with three goals and Billy Frampton’s stellar year continued. The AFL will be rapt to have Collingwood in the wildcard round with the likelihood of a Victorian opponent making it a certain success in its first season. Rowell rewrites what’s possible Because statistics don’t tell the whole story we will simply present Brownlow Medallist Matt Rowell’s numbers against the Giants and leave the rest to your imagination.



The midfielder had 40 disposals with 28 kicks and 12 handballs. He laid 16 tackles and had 17 clearances, gaining 881 metres for his team. In a week when his offsider Noah Anderson told this masthead how hard the midfield were working with the coaches to get back their buzz, Rowell returned to his best. Huge day: Suns star Matt Rowell. Getty Images Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Take-home assessments to be banned in radical HSC overhaul
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWHSC Take-home assessments to be banned in radical HSC overhaul Christopher Harris August 9, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A radical overhaul of the Higher School Certificate would bar year 12 students from completing unsupervised take-home assignments as Education Minister Prue Car vows to safeguard the integrity of the NSW education system from the threat of AI. The move comes after it was revealed the use of artificial intelligence was driving a sustained and elevated rate of misconduct in year 12 assessments, with more than 1000 cases of cheating in HSC school-based tasks recorded in 2025. NSW Education Minister Prue Car has asked NESA for a moratorium on take-home HSC assessment tasks due to the threat of AI. Dion Georgopoulos Car has written to the NSW Education Standards Authority (NESA) to ask for a “moratorium” on take-home assessment tasks. It is subject to advice from NESA, but is expected to start as soon as next term when current year 11 students begin their year 12 studies. “The value of the HSC as a highly trusted credential depends on it accurately reflecting student knowledge, ability, and understanding. That confidence will be undermined if assessment outputs can be produced without students performing the intellectual work that the course requires,” Car said in a letter to NESA chair, Professor Peter Shergold, last month.



Removing take-home assessment would be an interim measure and will form part of a broader review on the impact of AI on student learning, amid concerns that students are outsourcing the most basic of tasks to AI. The removal of take-home tasks makes NSW the first jurisdiction in Australia to do so. Car said the purpose of schooling was to build knowledge, judgment, resilience and critical thinking over time, but that faced being undermined if students were using AI. “The settings for the HSC have an impact on learning throughout high school. Where teachers and students know they face an offline environment in final exams, that will likely impact they way they are prepared for those exams,” she said. “If you want to run a marathon, you don’t practise on a computer. You don’t build grey matter by getting a computer to do the thinking for you.”



While educational analysts have acknowledged the capacity of AI to enhance learning, a report drawing on surveys of 3400 NSW teachers revealed this year students were using it to complete assignments as well as outsourcing thinking to AI to help them perform even low-stakes activities like class discussions. Car said it was better to put sensible safeguards in place as policymakers came to fully understand AI’s long-term impact on student learning. “We need to act now as the evidence continues to emerge,” she said.



Final exams account for 50 per cent of a student’s HSC mark, while school-based tasks comprise the remaining half. Until now, they comprise a mix of both in-class (such as in-class tests and speeches) and take-home assessment. When the interim measures are introduced, it is expected there will be some exceptions for subjects with major projects, such as art and technology. The HSC proposal is set to start at the beginning of next term. Dominic Lorrimer Some principals report moving away from take-home tasks in response to AI, while most have updated their assessment policies to warn students they must be able to prove work done outside the classroom and submitted for assessment is their own. “Teachers will continue to use standard monitoring, draft checkpoints, and oral reflections (viva voce) to ensure all submitted work genuinely reflects a student’s own learning and authentic understanding,” Oakhill College in Sydney’s northwest informed parents earlier this year.



All Saints College in Maitland warns students that teachers “may use a viva voce, examine the digital footprint of the document, ask for research notes and drafts as part of the investigation to discover the authenticity and originality of student work”. Of the 1270 total cases of cheating in HSC assessment tasks recorded last year, the majority of misconduct cases related to take-home tasks. Related Article Education AI poses ‘urgent threat’ to student learning and the HSC The HSC shake-up comes as higher education analysts warn entry to universities in Sydney has become increasingly competitive due to funding changes. Next year will be worse, they say. Federal Education Minister Jason Clare said since the advent of widespread generative AI in 2022, the technology must be part of the education landscape, citing its ability to “personalise education”.



This year, Norway moved to implement a near total ban on primary school students using AI because of the risk pupils could skip important steps in their education. A similar push is under way in Australia. Last week, the Heads Up Alliance – an organisation that spearheaded the push to ban adolescents from using social media – launched a new campaign to stem the widespread use of tablets and laptops in Australian schools. A key principle of their campaign is that “Generative AI has no place in school learning”. “It turns out that Australia’s Digital Education Revolution of 2008 was, in effect, a vast experiment on our children. Today, the results of that experiment have become impossible to ignore,” founder Dany Elachi said. World.title: Paul Kelly, Snoop Dogg and you: A new kind of karaoke hits Melbourne
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life Paul Kelly, Snoop Dogg and you: A new kind of karaoke hits Melbourne Carolyn Webb August 9, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Inside one of Melbourne’s best-loved live music venues, a group of five people took a free and easy approach to singing Bruno Mars’ pop song 24K Magic at the weekend. They rapped, howled and laughed through the gently funky tune, making up lyrics while miraculously keeping up with the beat. Rocking good time: Five friends rapped and howled their way through a Bruno Mars song at Rockeoke. Martin Philbey In response, the crowd at St Kilda’s Esplanade Hotel on Saturday danced and cheered along, and took snaps with their phones. This is Rockeoke – a weekly karaoke session where people of all singing abilities get to live out their music dreams on stage with the backing of a live band.



By the end of the night, participants can brag they’ve performed at the Espy, where music royalty such as Paul Kelly, Snoop Dogg and AC/DC have also played. Singers, who can put their names down either online or at the basement bar on the night, have 65 songs to choose from, including INXS’s Never Tear Us Apart, Wonderwall by Oasis, and Billie Eilish’s Ocean Eyes. Dream gig: Niamh Troy (left) and Avalon Johnstone sang in the Espy basement bar, backed by a professional band. Martin Philbey If you request an off-list song such as Enter Sandman by Metallica the band is willing to give it a go, keyboard player Thomas Byrne said. On Saturday, one group took the “where do we go now?” line in Guns N’ Roses’ Sweet Child O’ Mine literally, missing lyrics and sometimes the melody, but they were laughing.



Guitarist Simon Paparo said “it’s not about singing perfectly”, but the band will guide singers towards a chorus or ending. Another performer, Eadiella, of Hampton, who goes by one name, smashed Amy Winehouse’s Back to Black out of the park, giving a tune and word-perfect rendition of the pop classic. Nailed it: Singer Eadiella belts out Amy Winehouse’s Back to Black. Martin Philbey Eadiella channelled Winehouse’s growling voice and threw herself into the song’s dramatic tale of romance gone wrong while the crowd swayed and sang along as if this were the Glastonbury Festival in England. Espy venue manager Dan Lovett said the idea for Rockeoke came after a Gaelic football club held its post-finals Mad Monday party at the Espy, and its karaoke session was a huge hit.



“It went off,” Lovett said. He said the event blended karaoke with the Espy’s strength – live rock music. About 36 singers now sign up to Rockeoke each week. The event is free and runs from 11pm for three hours each Saturday. “Each week the crowd’s getting bigger,” Lovett said. “You never know, in a few months it might be on the [Espy’s] main stage, in the Gershwin Room.”



People aged from 18 to 80 have sung in Rockeoke since it began, he said. One week, an 80-year-old sang the 1968 psychedelic rock song Fire by obscure British band The Crazy World of Arthur Brown – famous for the line “I am the god of hellfire!” Lovett said the nice thing about karaoke and Rockeoke is that “even if it’s bad, it’s good. As long as you get up there and have a crack, you’re going to have a great time.”

World.title: After Elizabeth, Redeemer Baptist Church was banned from taking in children of the state. Instead, it opened a school
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWPrivate schools After Elizabeth, Redeemer Baptist Church was banned from taking in children of the state. Instead, it opened a school Emily Kowal August 9, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There’s gravel from Redeemer Baptist School’s property burrowed deep inside Elizabeth Bradbury’s knee. The 62-year-old only has to touch the gnarled skin to be transported back to the 1970s and ’80s, when at 15, screaming for her mum during a planned visit, as she was pulled away by male members of Redeemer Baptist Church. “I got dragged by my hair because I fought them off,” she said. When she stumbled, she fell into the gravel driveway. Elizabeth Bradbury at the Australian Botanic Gardens in Mt Annan. Elizabeth Bradbury was one of the first children to be placed into the care of Redeemer Baptist Church. Sitthixay Ditthavong In 1976, when Bradbury was 11, she was placed into the care of elders at Redeemer Baptist Church by the Youth and Community Services officers with the consent of her mother, who surrendered her care to Redeemer.



By the time Bradbury left in 1981, aged 16 and in the middle of her HSC year, the department of youth and community services banned Redeemer Baptist Community from caring for children in need of substitute care. But Redeemer did not stop caring for children. Instead, the church became a school, operating at first as an unregistered community school, before being accredited by the Department of Education in 1983. On Monday, the school will be at the centre of a NSW Parliamentary inquiry, after a slew of “disturbing” allegations unveiled by this masthead and 60 Minutes into the academically acclaimed private school. Redeemer Baptist School will face a parliamentary inquiry on Monday. Wolter Peeters The school in North Parramatta is accused of subjecting its students to extreme control, dictating their underwear colour and university choices, and not paying its teachers wages.



The school, which has an extensive property portfolio, had raked in tens of millions in government funding in the past decade – all while its teachers go unpaid, relying on a small stipend and, for some, Centrelink benefits. Since the school began, at least 50 children have lived in the homes of church elders Jonathan Cannon and Russell Bailey. A photo of Elizabeth Bradbury taken at around 15 years old. She was suffering during this time and desperately wished to leave the church. But Bradbury wants the world to know that these allegations are not new. She says Redeemer’s alleged control of children started long before its current leaders, Cannon and Bailey were in power. The church was founded by Noel Cannon, Jonathan’s father and a former science head at The King’s School, who was an esteemed figure within the Castle Hill and Parramatta community. When he died in 2012, his life was described in parliament as one of “uncompromising love”.



Bradbury remembers a much darker picture. Despite her mother giving up her care, both wanted to continue contact. She said she was only allowed to see her mother once or twice a year. Placed inside the Baileys home – alongside a teenage Russell Bailey, now the school’s headmaster – she described a life of strict surveillance and control. She was not allowed to use tampons. The wife of a senior church elder once checked under her skirt to make sure. “I was standing on something, and she ran her hands up and down my legs. She realised I was shaving my legs,” she said. She was reprimanded.“When I got my period, [she] basically said if you use tampons, you’re no longer a virgin,” Bradbury said. At the time, Bradbury recalls, there were a number of foster children living inside Redeemer. One of them was a girl who had schizophrenia. Bradbury remembers watching elders hold the girl down while they performed what she described as an exorcism. “She was resisting, fighting them off, and they just held her down while they prayed for her,” Bradbury recalled. “She was psychotic, and I watched that. I witnessed that.“ Redeemer Baptist School leaders, principal Jonathan Cannon and headmaster Russell Bailey.



Any defiance was dealt with by Noel Cannon. At the time, church members attended nearby Castle Hill High School, allowing them to make friends outside the Redeemer community. Bradbury recalls wanting to leave the church in her senior years. Letters, written during that time and kept by Bradbury, show her pleading with an old friend to help her escape. Labelled “rebellious” because she wanted to return to her mother and study nursing, Bradbury was taken upstairs to Noel’s office. As Bradbury lay crying on the floor, Noel loomed over her. “He pulled me up by my hair and I ended up with my head between his legs, and I said to him, ‘You don’t want to do this’,” she said. He let her go, she said. When Bradbury heard Cannon being praised in parliament, she vomited. “I had my head between that man’s legs,” she said. Sam Gibson has his own memories inside Noel Cannon’s office. Adopted into the church in 1974, Gibson spent much of his childhood terrified of Noel Cannon. For years, he was moved between homes, living with different families, among overseas students and “stragglers”.



He estimates he was caned by Noel Cannon upwards of 50 times. Cannon’s son, a then teenage Jonathan Cannon, would often be in the room, watching on. “If I did something wrong or looked at Jon Cannon the wrong way … I was marched up to his dad and his dad put me over the pew, giving me three of the best,” he said. When Gibson was sexually assaulted by another member of the church as a child, Noel Cannon confronted Gibson. “He came up to me and said, ‘You’ve got a dirty little secret don’t you? You are going to sit over there until you tell me what it is’,” Gibson said. Sam Gibson was adopted into Redeemer Baptist School Wayne Taylor



When Gibson left in 1992, Noel Cannon issued a threat: “Sam, if you ever mention anything of what has happened in here or goes on in here, I’ll come down on you like a ton of bricks,” Gibson recalled. Gibson said Redeemer was “not a place of love, of care. It’s a place of control, fear, humiliation”. Bradbury was horrified to learn the church that “destroyed” her has taken in more than 50 more children since the school began. “This is no different to what happened back then … these people are still succumbing to this thing,” Bradbury said. Bradbury wants the school to sell everything it owns to pay back people she said it has harmed.



“I’m not alone anymore, and there’s people there that need to get out too. They need to be finished,” he said. Redeemer did not respond to the Herald’s questions. In a previous statement, the school said: “Just because our practices are unfamiliar, it does not mean they are unlawful, coercive or abusive, and we reject the attempt to portray us as anything other than a law-abiding community with strong Christian faith and practices”. Related Investigation

Private schools Redeemer Baptist School investigation The NSW inquiry, which Redeemer representatives will not attend, will examine “any use by the school of coercive control in relation to students, families, guardians, employees and volunteers”. The inquiry has received more than 100 submissions, many from current volunteer teachers.



“The flavour of Christianity that was taught was fire and brimstone on acid and as students we were left in zero doubt about where they stood on key issues, particularly on matters such as equal rights for all, and marriage equality as cases in point,” wrote ex-student Danny Nowlan in one submission. “We were told in no uncertain terms if we were to date fellow school students we would be suspended/expelled”. It is not the first time the school has found itself in the halls of parliament. In 2007, Greens MP John Kaye called for an inquiry into the school after accusing the school of an “extraordinary tax sham and welfare fraud” that has cost the federal government more than $1 million, state parliament heard. The chair of Monday’s inquiry, Greens MP Abigail Boyd, said: “This is a school that is supposedly overseen by NSW authorities and has benefited from public funds. Serious allegations and concerns were raised decades ago and never resolved by public officials. The community deserves answers, and that’s what our inquiry will seek to provide.”

World.title: Car clash: Private vehicles and the true price the nation pays
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life Car clash: Private vehicles and the true price the nation pays Cassandra Morgan August 9, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A divisive study has laid bare the true price of Australia’s huge number of private cars, finding they cost the country at least $316 billion a year – and the public foots half the bill. University of Queensland researchers say they are the first to fully quantify the “car economy” across five states, and expose a whopping annual estimated cost of $158 billion to the wider public. The study found drivers directly paid only half the annual cost of the vehicle economy. Pat Scala The huge public bill is the total of everything from congestion to the cost of car parks and roads, emissions, pollution and collisions. “Cars impose all these costs on society,” said Associate Professor Dorina Pojani of the university’s School of Architecture, Design and Planning. “People think of automobility, and they just think of the actual car that they drive. But automobility is a whole system.”



Cars impose hidden costs on society says urban planning expert Dr Dorina Pojani. Pojani said she was motivated to investigate the cost of Australia’s car use after robust discussions with her students, who were adamant that drivers paid their way. “They’d say: ‘Yeah, but drivers, we pay lots of fees and taxes, and for fuel, etc.’” Related Article City life ‘Taking the mickey’: Inner-city council tears up e-bike deal The study, though, revealed drivers directly paid only half the annual cost of the vehicle economy (49.82 per cent, or an estimated $157.48 billion) in fuel, parking, tolls and buying vehicles. The wider public, including people who, like Pojani, don’t drive, bore the remainder of the cost (50.18 per cent, or an estimated $158.64 billion).



The public cost outweighed the private cost in all states except NSW. “To this day, I just never got used to cars,” said Pojani, who grew up in communist-era Albania when private car ownership was banned. She now lives in Brisbane. The direct cost to drivers includes expenses such as buying vehicles and paying for fuel, parking and tolls. Drivers also help foot the public bill. Melbourne resident Luke Sapwell, who relies on public transport. Joe Armao Most people living in cities have a choice to drive or catch public transport. The same can’t be said for trucks, which are necessary to move food and other goods around Australia, Pojani said. They were excluded on that basis from the study, which looked at cars and light commercial vehicles only.



But the point of the research wasn’t to cast blame on drivers, for many of whom cars were also a necessity, Pojani said. Instead, the study used a Harvard University-tested method to encourage Australian governments to “put their money where their mouth is” on sustainability. Related Article Public transport ‘Too many cars, too much traffic’: Fuel crisis puts spotlight on car dependency “If [governments are] going to subsidise transport, they need to subsidise the right kind of transport, which is public transport, micromobility, meaning bicycle lanes, bicycle parking,” Pojani said. “My hunch is that the whole car industry knows that they’re getting a pretty good deal in Australia. The figures are clear.” The subsidisation point rang true for Melbourne resident Luke Sapwell, who supports his tax dollars going to the likes of schools, although he doesn’t have children, or hospitals, even though he’s healthy.



The difference with cars was that, for many, driving is a choice, the 34-year-old finance broker and business owner said. Sapwell doesn’t have a car, works mainly from home and relies on public transport and shared e-bikes to get around. That was until his local council, the City of Yarra, voted last month to tear up a deal with US-headquartered hiring company Lime, ordering e-bikes off the area’s streets in inner Melbourne. “Having half of car user costs being borne by other people – that’s unfair,” said Sapwell. Sapwell says governments should consider taxpayers’ subsidisation of cars when weighing up whether to support greener alternatives, such as shared e-bikes. Joe Armao “The least vulnerable people in our community can afford to use cars.



“So really, I just cannot even comprehend why we would be further disadvantaging vulnerable people in our community by taking away such an obvious mode of transport [share bikes] that has minimal impacts on the environment.” National Roads and Motorists’ Association spokesman Peter Khoury said the University of Queensland research had a fatal flaw. While it analysed the costs of Australia’s car economy, it was silent as to its benefits. Related Article City life Answer in 10 seconds or lose your fleet: The e-bike row dividing Yarra “You wouldn’t let your kids set up a lemonade stand without doing a cost-benefit analysis,” Khoury said. “The benefit to 100 years of investing in infrastructure for the combustion engine has helped basically carry Australia to one of the best standards-of-living nations on the face of the earth.



“Bureaucrats are not going to look at a report that quantifies the cost without quantifying the benefit.” Different approaches could quantify the cost of Australia’s car economy differently, Pojani said. But, even if there was a margin of error, the researchers were talking about billions of dollars. “We’re not talking about pennies,” Pojani said. The researchers’ findings were published in the peer-reviewed scientific journal Proceedings of the Institution of Civil Engineers. World.title: I’ve succeeded because of my public school education, not despite it
World.content:
NationalNSWEducation Opinion I’ve succeeded because of my public school education, not despite it Farzam Zaher Economist August 9, 2026 — 7:30pm

August 9, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Parenting involves a lot of tricky choices. Not least of which is where your child should go to school. Parents are increasingly finding themselves in a strategic game to optimise their child’s future by increasing their odds at getting into a better school – whether that be public, selective, Catholic or independent. Glebe Public School parents addressed falling enrolments by creating a document focusing on the school’s strengths, including the band. Sitthixay Ditthavong Increasingly, parents have turned away from our public schools. It’s no secret that enrolments in our public schools are declining. Before the pandemic, 65 per cent of NSW students attended a public school. In 2025, it was down to 62 per cent, and the total number of students enrolled has declined by more than 30,000 over the same time.



There are many reasons given to explain this decline. An oft-cited one is that for many parents looking to give their kids the best shot at life, public schools are just not as good as private options and so many parents have chosen to switch. Related Article Education Parents pour more than $4.5 billion into private and Catholic schools every year With some shelling out over $500,000 for the state’s top private schools, it can be an expensive choice too. In all fairness, the choice can seem rather obvious. Private schools boast excellent facilities, extensive options for extracurricular and co-curricular activities and go toe-to-toe with the top selective schools in annual HSC results league tables. Indeed, analysis by The Australian Financial Review revealed that more than half of Australia’s prime ministers went to either a private or Catholic school. So, to set your child on the path to greatness, put them in a private school (unless you don’t want a politician in the family, fair enough). It’s a no-brainer, right?



Not quite. The data says, “It just ain’t so.” Of course, most public schools can’t compete on the grounds of, well, school grounds. And to try to keep up with their private counterparts on extracurricular activities, some schools, such as Sydney Boys High School, ask for an annual voluntary contribution of $3000. But when you look at educational attainment, the picture looks quite different. A 2022 study of NAPLAN results, conducted by researchers from the University of New England, found that once a student’s background is accounted for (such as socioeconomic status and parents’ education attainment), there was no significant benefit for independent and Catholic school students over public school students. Other studies looking at student performance at university have largely found that students who went to public high schools do just as well, if not better, than their privately educated peers. It seems then that perhaps independent schools are less a guaranteed booster to a better life, but rather an aggregator of postcodes and parental attitudes towards education.



Related Article Education The public parents fighting the flight to private school If you have sent your child down the private education path, it is easy to attribute any future success to the school. It becomes tricky to account for the fact that your concern for their education and your encouragement for them to learn and grow as people is what can make a real difference. A student’s attitude towards their learning, motivation and self-discipline – often shaped by the parents – is a big driver of academic success. These qualities are not inherent to the school but develop first at home. It can explain why students from public schools can outperform their privately educated peers at university. Private school students benefit from a halo effect from their peers, but extensive support directly from the school to boost HSC results can negatively affect independent learning skills that are critical for succeeding in university. There are other benefits to public schools that aren’t reflected in the numbers.



Public schools bring together and reflect the local community, often from diverse backgrounds, which helps children develop key soft skills in interacting with people from all walks of life. At a time when Australia seems increasingly divided, this is becoming even more important. Needless to say, your teachers also matter. Our public school teachers and staff are dedicated and deliver the best possible education for students of all abilities, as do their private school peers. Then again, I may be biased. When my family first arrived in Australia, a private school was never on the cards, but my parents prioritised education and wanted my siblings and I to do well. They taught me to value my education, which in turn drove me to study hard. For this, I will always be grateful to my parents. Along the way, I have been helped by countless dedicated teachers. One teacher encouraged me to apply for the NSW Education Minister’s Student Council, and so in Year 11, I found myself advising the minister and the Department of Education. My economics teacher read countless drafts of my application for a cadetship in financial services. Thanks to his help, at 17 I began working in the industry while studying economics at the University of Sydney.



At 21, I have made it this far not despite my public education, but because of it. Farzam Zaher is a Dalyell Scholar and casual academic at the University of Sydney. He attended government schools in Wollongong.

World.title: Two arrested after fleeing vehicle collides with police car
World.content:
Two people have been arrested after a car crashed into two vehicles, including a police car, and swerved around road spikes near Palmerston North this evening.

Whanganui Area Commander Inspector Ash Gurney said police sighted a vehicle of interest in the Marton area about 4.30pm, and signalled for it to stop.

"The driver failed to do so, and officers did not pursue due to the manner of driving."

Inspector Gurney said the vehicle then fled towards Whanganui on State Highway 3.

"Officers set up road spikes. However, the vehicle avoided them and continued to flee. Due to the manner of driving and associated risks, officers did not pursue the vehicle."

Leaving Whanganui, the vehicle collided with a police car at low speed.

No injuries were reported, but the police car was damaged to the point that it was undriveable.

Police sighted the vehicle again about 6pm travelling south through Bulls and more attempts to spike the vehicle were unsuccessful.

About 6.25pm, police said the vehicle was involved in a crash near Levin, but continued driving. No injuries had been reported.

Just after 7pm, police received a call reporting the vehicle had hit a fence at Rangiotu, and two occupants were taken into custody.

World.title: St John confirms weekly all-time call record has been broken again
World.content:
A spike in winter illnesses is being blamed for Hato Hone St John recording its busiest single day on record.

The ambulance service has now activated its major incident response to cope with sustained high demand, which was expected to continue on Monday.

On Saturday, 2562 calls came into the ambulance service through 111 - the highest number received in a single day. A normal day would see around 1900 calls. There were 2079 calls to 111 for an ambulance by 5.45pm on Sunday.

As of 7.45pm on Sunday, the ambulance service had received 16,008 calls this week. That beat the previous record of 15,289 calls, set just a week earlier between 27 July and 2 August.

Before that, the busiest week on record had seen 14,984 calls. That record was set between 25 and 31 August in 2025.

Hato Hone St John director of ambulance operations Doug Gallagher said the "highly unusual" sudden spike in demand correlated with the recent cold snap, and there had been an influx in people requesting ambulances for winter illnesses such as influenza and respiratory issues.

"It has been a relatively mild winter, up until about a week, a week and a half ago.

"There does seem to be a correlation with the temperature, the weather. So from that perspective, there's a bit of hope that when the weather improves things can get back to normal."

While patients with broken bones, those who had fallen, and those not in life-threatening pain could expect to wait several hours for an ambulance, Gallagher said response times for the sickest patients remained within safe limits.

"During that time, though, all incidents are being managed and monitored. They are likely to receive callbacks from clinicians within our 111 centre and potentially, the problem can be managed over the phone with clinical advice or referral into other parts of health."

He said about 10 percent of the calls they received were dealt with over the phone, through a process called Hear and Advise.

On Saturday, 2562 calls came into the ambulance service through 111. St John / Supplied

Emergency services under pressure

Gallagher explained the ambulance service's concerns at a press conference on Sunday afternoon, where St John confirmed the major incident response following a difficult Saturday.

"At the peak, emergency call handlers were answering a call every 20 seconds," he said.

Multiple days in the past week "were busier than any recorded during the Covid-19 pandemic or on traditionally high-volume dates such as New Year's Eve", he said.

"Our emergency ambulance staff are continuing to respond effectively, but the workload is not showing the signs of easing that we would normally expect," he said on Sunday afternoon.

World.title: Wellington city councillor Tony Randle dies suddenly
World.content:
Local and national politicians are paying tribute to Wellington city councillor Tony Randle, who died suddenly at the weekend.

Councillor Randle, who represented the Takapū/Northern Ward, was first elected in 2022 and re-elected in 2025.

He served on a number of committees and was appointed to the Wellington Regional Transport Committee. Earlier this week he voted with city councillors agreed to submit a super-merger proposal to the government this weekend.

Wellington mayor Andrew Little said Randle's contribution to the council was marked by diligence, care and a commitment to understanding the detail.

"Tony was deeply committed to public service and wanted the best for Wellington and its communities. He was always cordial and constructive, but he also brought a healthy scepticism to every issue.

"He believed an important part of his role was to challenge, question, and test assumptions to ensure decisions were based on solid evidence.

"What really set him apart was his focus on substance over rhetoric. He wanted to understand the facts, examine the evidence, and make the best possible decision based on all available information.

"He was never willing to be rushed and valued thorough analysis and quality decision-making above all else. He applied his analytical skills to public transport in particular and was always willing to engage with the public on detailed and principles grounds."

He would be sorely missed around the council table, Little said.

"He was just one of those people that you knew when he was in a meeting, he was onto it, he was going to ask questions and he was all about ... doing the best that he could."

Little said discovering a $250 million error in council consultation documents on lowering the speed limit in 2023 exemplified his determination to dig into the details.

"He very much focused on the data and if he didn't think he had enough would ask for more, and what he found through that process and his hard work was that actually they had miscalculated some of the data and had come up with a conclusion that was out by $250 million."

There would be a by-election for councillor Randle's seat in due course, Little said.

Infrastructure Minister and Hutt South MP Chris Bishop described councillor Mr Randle as a lovely man who was passionate about Wellington.

Council chief executive Matt Prosser said Randle was a "strong and passionate advocate for his local community, engaging thoughtfully with residents and participating in public discussions on issues that mattered to Wellington".

World.title: Schools closed as Ohakune faces water shutdown
World.content:
Ohakune schools will be closed on Monday as the town grapples with a water shutdown caused by leaking pipes.

The Ruapehu District Council and water contractor Veolia are urging residents to conserve water, warning the town's reservoir is down to 12 percent.

A council spokesperson said the leak, caused by last month's earthquake, was discovered on Thursday and repaired the following day, but the need to remove air from the water line had delayed the fix.

The council had brought in port-a-loos and was providing tankers of drinking water, but stressed that they were for homes and essential services, and businesses may need to close.

"The reservoir has been drained, so it takes time for that reservoir to refill and then for the treatment to come through," Horizons Regional Council chair Nikki Riley said.

"But until then, the good people of Tongariro Water will be supplying water for the township."

Tap water was not expected to be restored until 5pm Monday. If restored before then, the water would need to be boiled before use, the council said.

It warned against using public toilets.

Drinking water was available at various locations around the town, it said.

Nearly 1400 people live in Ohakune, but the population can double or treble during the ski season.

Drinking water

Bottled water: Ruapehu District Council office, 38 Ayr St; Thames St opposite the Powderhorn; Goldfinch St/Shannon St corner; rear car park of the Ohakune iSite; Clyde St car park; Moore St outside Top 10 Holiday Park.

Water tanker: Council office. Please reuse empty 5-litre bottles and refill them there.

World.title: Companies must adapt to rising AI costs, tech commentator says
World.content:
The cheap or free use of AI tools is over.

"For the last three years, the most expensive experiment in technology history has run on someone else's money," Fusion5 chief executive Kristy Brown said.

A white paper released by technology services provider Fusion5 sets out the case for a managed approach to the running of AI agents in order to avoid runaway costs, while maintaining compliance with emerging regulatory requirements as well as institutional risks to businesses.

"Who's paying for AI now? Increasingly, it's you," Brown said, adding that many AI agents were adopting a pay-by-token system rather than an all-you-can-eat user licence, or a hybrid scheme which combined a bit of both.

These include Anthropic's Claude, Google's Gemini, Microsoft's CoPilot and many other widely used coding and customer service agents.

"Prior to this phase of our AI revolution, initially it was just about trying to get people to trust and to use AI," Brown said.

She said the challenge now was to use AI more efficiently, with smart processes that improved search accuracy and resulted in fast results.

"Usage-based pricing means every prompt, every reasoning step and every autonomous agent now carries a real, metered cost - and someone must pay it," she said.

"Autonomous agents now commit spend, reconcile transactions and make decisions that bind the organisation. They're also expensive in a way traditional software never was."

She said AI agents reason in loops and can consume an order of magnitude beyond a simple query.

"An agent stuck in a reasoning loop… can generate substantial costs before anyone notices."

She said AI agents needed monitoring and controls or risked landing businesses with a large bill and a nasty governance surprise.

"The businesses that build the discipline to operate AI - not just deploy it - will be the ones still standing when the music, and the free money, stops."

She said the key to improved performance was to collect key business processes in an "ontology", which was industry jargon for a rich, structured description of the underlying business model, including relationships to such things as a company description, the names and titles of senior executives, financial results, and small details like the font and colour of the business brand.

"It's the stuff that sits in your very deep experts' heads.

"And if you take the time to get those things right, it's a fast track way for your AI workloads to be able to get to the end outcome without a lot of these reasoning steps that it has to do if you haven't told it explicitly where to reference that information."

Brown said companies with incomplete data or digitised institutional knowledge were paying to ask AI agents to look for information that wasn't available, beyond the knowledge held by experienced staff.

"Without a shared meaning layer, businesses pay twice: once for the extra compute, and again for the mistake."

She said the transformation was already underway.

Global giants Tesla, Uber, Meta and Amazon were already implementing employee restrictions on AI Agent usage as businesses shift to the traditional model of measuring costs against productivity gains.

"The four biggest US tech firms are on track to spend close to US$700 billion on AI infrastructure this year alone. OpenAI reportedly spends around US$60 billion a year on compute against roughly US$13 billion of revenue. That gap has been a gift to the rest of us," Brown said.

"That gift was being withdrawn."

Microsoft was leading the pack in driving revenue gains through licensing of its AI Agent Copilot, which was an integral piece of its suite of Office tools, according to its latest fourth quarter earnings report.

"This year, Azure revenue surpassed US$100 billion for the first time, and Microsoft 365 Copilot reached over 30 million paid seats, reflecting the confidence customers are placing in us to power their AI transformation," Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella said.

Global giants Tesla, Uber, Meta and Amazon are already implementing employee restrictions on AI Agent usage. Moor Studio

The case for an agent operations centre (AOC)

Brown said there was a case for a dedicated function that watched every agent in real time, tracked cost per agent with thresholds and alerts, monitored each agent's guard rails, and escalated to a human the moment an agent stepped out of line.

"This is exactly why Fusion5 is investing in building an Agent Operations Centre," Brown said, adding the service would be officially launched in the fourth quarter of the year, with 1400 existing customers in the New Zealand and Australian region.

She said an AOC was aimed at helping small to mid-sized businesses, who don't have the in-house expertise to manage themselves.

"For a business without Silicon Valley's balance sheet, that math matters even more."

She said the proliferation of AI assistants or agents had introduced a class of operational challenges that conventional IT management was never designed to address.

"Business functions that rely on autonomous agents for critical workflows cannot simply revert to manual processes when agents fail or are unavailable," the white paper says.

World.title: Deadline for local council amalgamation plans arrives
World.content:
The future of New Zealand's councils is now in the government's hands, with time running out to submit an amalgamation proposal.

Sunday was the deadline to pitch a Head Start plan for creating larger unitary councils.

Those who have not done so will now have one forced on them under the Back Stop process.

Officials will now assess the proposals - including whether it is realistic and delivers better value to ratepayers.

Approved plans will be signed off in 2027, with the Back Stop process finalised in the same year.

The changes are expected to take effect from the 2028 local elections.

City v rural

Earlier this week, Hamilton District Council voted 12 to three to not participate - meaning the district would end up in a backstop process controlled by central government to ensure reforms still went ahead. Down south, Christchurch City Council unanimously agreed to submit on the Head Start process. Wellington and Wairarapa mayors have agreed to put two amalgamation proposals to ministers.

In the Manawatū-Whanganui, five councils have agreed to work together on a work programme, rather than submit a plan for amalgamation.

Palmerston North and Horowhenua have proposed a new sub-regional council, but Whanganui mayor Andrew Tripe says it - along with Rangitīkei, Tararua, Manawatū, and Ruapheu - have chosen an alternative option.

Tripe said the council was not going to let the government decide what it was going to do.

He said it was not against local government reform, but needed more time to consult with the community, as well as consider what financial constraints the council would face.

Nearly 90 percent of those surveyed by Manawatū District Council were opposed to amalgamating.

Mayor Michael Ford said 86 percent of the 750 people who responded to the survey were against amalgamating with any other councils in the Manawatū-Whanganui region.

He said more than half refused to answer who they would prefer to join with if forced, while 30 percent voted for Rangitīkei, and 10 percent for Palmerston North.

Ford said Manawatū's rural community were very opposed to amalgamating with Palmerston North, as they did not want city people telling them how to run their farms.

On announcing the three-month Head Start process in May, Local Government Minister Simon Watts and Resource Management Act Reform Minister Chris Bishop had a stark message for councils.

"Today we are giving council's a clear choice. Lead your own reform or we will do it for you," Bishop said.

In a post on social media this morning, former prime minister Helen Clark said it had been a "haphazard approach" to local government amalgamation, driven by current government.

World.title: 'Great concerns' for missing Whanganui woman, police say
World.content:
Police are seeking help from the public to find a 59-year-old woman reported missing from Whanganui.

The woman, Sharon, was last seen on Monday, 27 July around 11am, near Kent Road in Saint Johns Hill.

"Police and Sharon's family have great concerns for her welfare and would like to find her as soon as possible," authorities wrote in a post on social media on Sunday.

"We believe she is still in the Whanganui area, however she has links to Auckland, and could also be in the wider Auckland area."

World.title: Rising Aussie UFC star calls for tougher fighters after first-round win
World.content:
The moment was not too big for Quillan Salkilld.

Making his main event debut, the Australian's run of first-round finishes continued on Saturday night local time in Las Vegas as he defeated veteran Mateusz Gamrot with a rear-naked choke at 4:25 of the first round of their non-title lightweight bout at UFC Fight Night at the UFC APEX.

Salkilld (13-1) survived a Gamrot (26-5) leg-lock during an extensive grappling exchange in the scheduled five-round fight before working to the back and locking in the finish, earning the biggest victory of his career while extending his winning streak to 13 fights.

Salkilld, who has now won his past four fights and five of his last six in the first round, called for a step up in competition after the victory.

"I think I deserve someone who's in the top five or close to it," Salkilld said.

Following the victory, the number 12-ranked Salkilld positioned himself for a match-up near the top of the lightweight division, while the number eight-ranked Gamrot absorbed a setback against one of the division's fastest-rising contenders.

Saturday's event marked the UFC's return to Las Vegas after two events abroad, in Abu Dhabi on July 25 and then Belgrade last Saturday.

In the co-main event, Diego Ferreira (20-7 MMA) landed more than 135 significant strikes across 15 minutes to earn a unanimous decision against Billy Quarantillo (18-8 MMA) in their lightweight bout.

All three judges scored the fight 30-27 for Ferreira, who kept Quarantillo on the defensive in Quarantillo's first Octagon appearance in more than 600 days after suffering a knee injury and his first lightweight fight since 2017.

Darren Elkins's UFC retirement fight ended unceremoniously as Yadier del Valle (11-1 MMA) needed one left hook to secure a TKO stoppage 35 seconds into the opening round of their featherweight bout.

Del Valle quickly closed the show against Elkins (29-13 MMA), spoiling the longtime veteran's final Octagon appearance while rebounding from the first loss of his career in February.

"I'm thankful for it all … don't ever give up on yourself," Elkins said following the loss.

Strawweight Alexia Thainara (15-1) utilised a relentless pace and a variety of take-downs alongside unorthodox striking to earn a unanimous decision against former strawweight contender Amanda Lemos (15-7-1), taking the cards 29-28, 29-28 and 30-27 in their all-Brazilian match-up.

Unbeaten welterweight Ty Miller (8-0 MMA) opened the main card by stopping Billy Ray Goff (9-5 MMA) via TKO 15 seconds into the third round.

Miller unleashed punches against the fence to force the stoppage, extending his perfect professional record while handing Goff his third straight defeat.
